1.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part one.

scenes.say: Most beginners lose money in crypto by breaking three simple rules.
Rule one: only invest money you can afford to lose. Not your rent, not your savings.
Crypto can drop fifty percent in just a few weeks.
If that would keep you up at night, you're investing too much.
Rule two: start with the giants. Bitcoin and Ethereum have survived every crash.
Random coins promising a thousand x? That's where most beginners get burned.
Rule three: don't go all in. Buy a small, fixed amount every week. It's called D.C.A.
You stop guessing the bottom, and your average price smooths out.
Follow for part two: how to choose a safe exchange. Not financial advice.

2.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part two.

scenes.say: In 2022, FTX, one of the biggest crypto exchanges in the world, collapsed in a few days, and customers couldn't withdraw their money.
scenes.p: A huge futuristic crypto exchange building with its glass doors chained shut and padlocked, a crowd of worried people outside, the wolf in front looking up at it with a serious face, dark rainy night.

scenes.say: So here's how to choose a safer exchange. First, check that it's regulated or registered where you live.
scenes.p: The wolf inspects a grand bank-like crypto exchange building with a big magnifying glass, a shiny golden shield emblem on the facade, sunny day.

scenes.say: Second, turn on two-factor authentication the moment you sign up. A password alone is not enough.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a smartphone glowing with a big blue shield and padlock icon, while a hooded hacker silhouette is blocked behind a thick glass wall.

scenes.say: Third, look at the fees. Trading fees, spreads and withdrawal fees add up fast.
scenes.p: The wolf frowns at a very long paper receipt unrolling down to the floor, while small gold coins leak out of a hole in his money bag.

scenes.say: Fourth, test the withdrawal. Send a small amount out before you send anything big.
scenes.p: The wolf carefully drops one single small gold coin into a glowing futuristic transfer tube, watching it travel, focused expression.

scenes.say: And remember: an exchange is a place to buy, not always the best place to store.
scenes.p: The wolf walks out of a crypto exchange building carrying a small steel safe under his arm, confident smile, city street.

scenes.say: Follow for part three: hot wallets versus cold wallets. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a confident grin, holding a flaming smartphone in one hand and an icy frozen hardware wallet in the other.

3.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part three.

scenes.say: Where you keep your crypto matters as much as what you buy.
scenes.p: The wolf stands between two doors: one door on fire and one door covered in ice, thinking with a paw on his chin, neon city corridor.

scenes.say: A hot wallet is an app on your phone or computer. It's connected to the internet, so it's fast and easy to use.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a smartphone that glows bright orange with small flames around it, crypto coins flying out of the screen.

scenes.say: It's great for small amounts you use often, but it's more exposed to hackers and malware.
scenes.p: A shadowy hooded hacker hand reaches out of a laptop screen toward the wolf's glowing phone, the wolf pulls the phone away just in time.

scenes.say: A cold wallet keeps your keys offline, usually on a small hardware device.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a small hardware wallet device covered in frost and ice crystals, cold blue light, snowflakes around.

scenes.say: It's slower to use, but much harder to hack. That's why it's made for long-term savings.
scenes.p: A small hardware wallet resting inside a massive bank vault with a thick round steel door, the wolf guarding the vault with arms crossed.

scenes.say: A simple setup: spending money in a hot wallet, and the rest in cold storage.
scenes.p: The wolf at a desk with a small burning wooden box holding a few coins on the left and a huge icy steel vault full of coins on the right.

scenes.say: Follow for part four: the seed phrase rule nobody should ever break. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: Close-up of the wolf pointing at the viewer, holding an old paper scroll with a glowing golden key drawn on it.

4.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part four.

scenes.say: If someone gets these twelve words, your crypto is gone. Forever.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a small paper card with a grid of twelve small blank boxes, looking worried, a dark shadowy thief silhouette lurking behind him.

scenes.say: When you create a wallet, you get a seed phrase: usually twelve or twenty-four words.
scenes.p: The wolf at a desk writing carefully on a small paper card with a pen, a hardware wallet next to it, warm desk lamp.

scenes.say: Those words are the master key. Anyone who has them can move your coins from anywhere in the world.
scenes.p: A giant glowing golden master key floating above a globe, a sneaky masked thief grabbing it, the wolf shocked.

scenes.say: So never type them into a website. Never send them in a chat. And never save them in a screenshot.
scenes.p: The wolf with arms crossed and a stern face in front of a laptop, a smartphone and a camera, each one with a big red prohibition sign.

scenes.say: No real support team will ever ask for them. If someone does, it's a scam. Every single time.
scenes.p: A fake support agent wearing a smiling mask on a video call on a laptop, the wolf slams the laptop shut with an angry face.

scenes.say: Write them on paper, or stamp them on metal, and keep them somewhere safe.
scenes.p: The wolf stamps letters into a small steel plate with a hammer and metal punch, a home safe open behind him.

scenes.say: Follow for part five: what Bitcoin actually is, explained simply. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin while holding a big shiny golden Bitcoin coin, neon city at night.

5.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part five.

scenes.say: Bitcoin, explained in under a minute. No tech jargon.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a giant glowing golden Bitcoin coin, holding a stopwatch, confident smile, futuristic city.

scenes.say: Bitcoin is digital money that no bank and no government controls.
scenes.p: The wolf stands on top of a giant floating golden Bitcoin above a city, tiny bank buildings far below, blue sky.

scenes.say: Every transaction is recorded on a public ledger called the blockchain, copied on thousands of computers around the world.
scenes.p: A glowing chain of connected cubes wrapping around planet Earth, linking thousands of small computers, the wolf watching from space.

scenes.say: To cheat, someone would have to overpower most of that network at once. That's what keeps it secure.
scenes.p: A tiny cartoon villain pushing with all his strength against a gigantic glowing wall of servers that doesn't move, the wolf laughing.

scenes.say: And there will only ever be twenty-one million bitcoin. Nobody can print more.
scenes.p: The wolf locks a huge vault filled with a big pile of golden Bitcoin coins, heavy chains and a giant padlock, dramatic light.

scenes.say: That fixed supply is why some people call it digital gold. But its price can still swing a lot, so it's a high-risk investment.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a shiny gold bar in one paw and a golden Bitcoin in the other, balancing them like a scale, while a stormy price chart rages behind him.

scenes.say: Follow for part six: Ethereum, and why it's not just another coin. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a confident grin, a glowing purple-blue Ethereum crystal floating next to him.

6.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part six.

scenes.say: If Bitcoin is digital gold, Ethereum is a world computer.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a gigantic glowing Ethereum diamond crystal that works like a futuristic supercomputer with cables and lights.

scenes.say: Ethereum is a blockchain that can run programs, called smart contracts.
scenes.p: The wolf types on a holographic keyboard while glowing code blocks fly into a big Ethereum crystal, futuristic lab.

scenes.say: A smart contract works like a vending machine: the right input gives you the result automatically. No middleman.
scenes.p: The wolf inserts a coin into a sleek futuristic vending machine and a glowing package drops out automatically, no shopkeeper around.

scenes.say: That's how lending, trading and collectible apps run on Ethereum.
scenes.p: A floating futuristic city of small app buildings sitting on top of a giant Ethereum diamond platform, the wolf flying above with a jetpack.

scenes.say: Its coin, ether, pays the network fees, called gas.
scenes.p: The wolf at a futuristic gas station filling up a sports car with glowing purple fuel shaped like the Ethereum diamond.

scenes.say: In 2022, Ethereum switched to proof of stake and cut its energy use by more than ninety-nine percent.
scenes.p: The wolf plants a small green tree next to a glowing green Ethereum diamond, a huge old power plant shutting down in the background.

scenes.say: Follow for part seven: stablecoins, the crypto that's not supposed to move. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin, a calm green coin with a dollar sign floating perfectly still next to him.

7.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part seven.

scenes.say: Not all crypto goes up and down. Some coins are built to stay at one dollar.
scenes.p: The wolf balances a shiny green coin with a dollar sign perfectly on one fingertip, while other coins bounce wildly around him.

scenes.say: They're called stablecoins, like USDT and USDC. Each one aims to equal one US dollar.
scenes.p: A perfectly balanced scale with a green dollar-sign coin on one side and a paper dollar bill on the other, the wolf nodding.

scenes.say: Traders use them to park money between trades.
scenes.p: The wolf parks a sports car shaped like a big green coin in a neon parking garage, relaxed.

scenes.say: Most are backed by reserves, like cash and treasury bills, held by the issuer.
scenes.p: A big bank vault with neat stacks of cash and documents, an auditor with a clipboard checking them, the wolf watching.

scenes.say: But stable doesn't mean risk-free. In 2022, TerraUSD lost its peg and collapsed to almost zero.
scenes.p: A cracked coin falling off a cliff edge into darkness, the wolf on the edge with a shocked face.

scenes.say: So stick to the biggest, most transparent ones, and don't keep everything in one stablecoin.
scenes.p: The wolf calmly places coins into several different baskets lined up on a table.

scenes.say: Follow for part eight: why a cheap coin is not a cheap investment. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin, holding a tiny penny-like coin with a magnifying glass.

8.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part eight.

scenes.say: A coin that costs one cent is not cheaper than a coin that costs fifty thousand dollars.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a tiny copper coin in one paw and a giant golden coin in the other, raising an eyebrow, neon city.

scenes.say: Price alone tells you almost nothing. What matters is the market cap: the price, times the number of coins.
scenes.p: The wolf with a big calculator, multiplying a small coin by a huge mountain of coins, numbers floating as glowing symbols without text.

scenes.say: A coin at one cent, with a trillion coins in circulation, is already worth ten billion dollars.
scenes.p: A gigantic mountain of tiny copper coins as tall as skyscrapers, the wolf looking up at it in awe.

scenes.say: To reach just one dollar, it would need to be worth a trillion dollars. Only a handful of companies on Earth are worth that much.
scenes.p: A tiny copper coin trying to climb an impossibly tall ladder reaching into the clouds, the wolf laughing at the bottom.

scenes.say: So before you buy, check the market cap and the total supply, not just the price.
scenes.p: The wolf reads a tablet with a magnifying glass, looking smart and careful, desk with coins.

scenes.say: Follow for part nine: bull markets and bear markets, explained. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin, a golden bull and a big brown bear standing behind him.

9.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part nine.

scenes.say: Crypto moves in big seasons. Knowing which one you're in changes everything.
scenes.p: The wolf stands at a crossroads, on the left a sunny golden path with a charging bull, on the right a stormy path with a bear.

scenes.say: A bull market is when prices rise for months. Everyone is excited, and everyone feels like a genius.
scenes.p: The wolf rides a charging golden bull through a city street full of confetti and cheering crowds.

scenes.say: A bear market is when prices fall for months. People give up and say crypto is dead.
scenes.p: A big grumpy bear sitting on top of a red falling chart in the rain, the wolf standing calmly under an umbrella.

scenes.say: Bitcoin has gone through several of these cycles, with drops of seventy percent or more along the way.
scenes.p: The wolf hikes across a huge mountain range shaped like a price chart with high peaks and deep valleys.

scenes.say: The classic mistake: buying with excitement at the top, and selling in fear at the bottom.
scenes.p: Split scene: on the left the wolf happily buying at a mountain peak, on the right the same wolf crying at the bottom of a valley.

scenes.say: Patient investors often do the opposite. They keep buying slowly when everyone else is scared.
scenes.p: The wolf calmly stacks gold coins while a crowd of panicking people runs away in the background.

scenes.say: Follow for part ten: the Bitcoin halving. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin, a golden Bitcoin cut perfectly in half floating behind him.

10.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part ten.

scenes.say: Every four years or so, Bitcoin cuts its supply of new coins in half. It's called the halving.
scenes.p: A giant golden Bitcoin being sliced perfectly in half by a bright laser beam, the wolf watching with sunglasses.

scenes.say: New bitcoin are created as a reward for the miners who secure the network.
scenes.p: Cartoon miners with pickaxes inside a glowing digital mine extracting shiny Bitcoin coins, the wolf supervising with a hard hat.

scenes.say: That reward is cut in half about every four years. The last halving was in April 2024.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a big calendar page and a golden coin cut in half, celebrating with confetti.

scenes.say: So fewer new coins enter the market every day.
scenes.p: A golden faucet slowly dripping fewer and fewer Bitcoin coins into a bucket, the wolf watching closely.

scenes.say: In the past, big bull markets followed a halving. But past results don't guarantee future ones.
scenes.p: The wolf looks skeptically at an old rising chart on a dusty screen, scratching his head.

scenes.say: Around the year 2140, the last bitcoin will be mined. After that, no new ones, ever.
scenes.p: A far-future city in the year 2140 with flying cars, the very last golden Bitcoin falling into a jar, the wolf old with grey beard smiling.

scenes.say: Follow for part eleven: leverage, the fastest way to lose everything. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a serious look, a huge dangerous red lever behind him.

11.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part eleven.

scenes.say: Leverage can make you rich in a day, and broke in an hour.
scenes.p: The wolf pulls a giant red lever on a machine, half of the scene full of flying money, the other half empty and dark.

scenes.say: With leverage, you borrow to trade bigger. Ten times leverage means a hundred dollars controls a thousand.
scenes.p: The wolf tries to lift a gigantic barbell with tiny shaking arms, sweating.

scenes.say: Great when the price goes up. But a ten percent drop can wipe out your whole position.
scenes.p: The glass floor under the wolf's feet cracks and shatters, the wolf panicking.

scenes.say: That's called liquidation. The exchange closes your trade, and your money is gone.
scenes.p: A giant robotic arm sweeps a pile of gold coins off a table into a trash can, the wolf screaming.

scenes.say: Crypto can easily move ten percent in a day. With high leverage, a normal move becomes a total loss.
scenes.p: The wolf on a tiny surfboard being swept away by a gigantic red wave shaped like a price chart.

scenes.say: For beginners, the simplest rule is: no leverage. Only buy what you can pay for.
scenes.p: The wolf cuts a rope with scissors that tied him to a giant red balloon, landing safely on the ground, relieved.

scenes.say: Follow for part twelve: the stop loss, your seatbelt in trading. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin while fastening a seatbelt in a futuristic car.

12.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twelve.

scenes.say: Would you drive without a seatbelt? Then don't trade without a stop loss.
scenes.p: The wolf in a sports car fastening his seatbelt with a confident face, neon city highway at night.

scenes.say: A stop loss is an order that sells automatically if the price falls to a level you choose.
scenes.p: The wolf walks on a tightrope high above the city with a big safety net stretched below him.

scenes.say: You decide in advance how much you're willing to lose. For example, five percent.
scenes.p: The wolf draws a thick red horizontal line on a big trading screen with a marker, focused.

scenes.say: If the price hits that level, you're out. Small loss, no drama, no hoping.
scenes.p: The wolf falls from the tightrope and lands safely and softly in the safety net, giving a thumbs up.

scenes.say: Without one, a small loss can turn into a huge one while you're asleep.
scenes.p: The wolf sleeping peacefully in bed while a huge red chart crashes on a giant screen behind him.

scenes.say: Just don't set it too tight, or normal price swings will kick you out of good trades.
scenes.p: The wolf wobbling on an extremely thin thread, about to fall, nervous face.

scenes.say: Follow for part thirteen: taking profit, and why you need an exit plan. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin, standing next to a glowing green exit door.

13.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirteen.

scenes.say: Making money in crypto is the easy part. Keeping it is the hard part.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a bag of gold coins tightly while coins slip through a hole in the bottom, worried face.

scenes.say: Many people watched their coins double, waited for more, and gave it all back in the next crash.
scenes.p: The wolf watches sadly as a big balloon made of money floats away into the sky.

scenes.say: That's why you need an exit plan before you even buy.
scenes.p: The wolf draws a treasure-map-style plan on a big table with an arrow pointing to a door, planning carefully.

scenes.say: A simple one: sell a part at each target. For example, a quarter at two x, and another quarter at three x.
scenes.p: The wolf cuts a big golden cake shaped like a coin into four equal slices with a knife.

scenes.say: You lock in real gains, and you still keep some coins if the price keeps going up.
scenes.p: The wolf puts gold coins into a safe with one paw while still holding a few coins in the other, smiling.

scenes.say: Nobody sells at the exact top. The goal is to sell some, not to be perfect.
scenes.p: The wolf climbs a mountain and plants small flags at different heights on the way up, happy.

scenes.say: Follow for part fourteen: FOMO and FUD, the two emotions that empty wallets. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf points at the viewer with a grin, two cartoon emotion clouds behind him: one excited and one scared.

14.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part fourteen.

scenes.say: Two emotions empty more wallets than any market crash: FOMO and FUD.
FOMO is the fear of missing out. A coin pumps, everyone is posting about it, and you buy right at the top.
scenes.p: The wolf runs desperately after a rocket that has already launched into the sky, a crowd of people with phones cheering around.

scenes.say: FUD is fear, uncertainty and doubt. Scary news hits, and you panic sell at the bottom.
scenes.p: The wolf hides under his desk, trembling, while scary newspapers with big red warning symbols fly around the room.

scenes.say: Both make you act fast, without a plan. And that's exactly when mistakes happen.
The fix: decide your entries and exits before you even open the app.
And if you feel a strong urge to buy or sell right now, wait twenty-four hours.
Follow for part fifteen: how to spot a crypto scam in seconds. Not financial advice.

15.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part fifteen.

scenes.say: Crypto scams steal billions every year. Here's how to spot most of them in seconds.
scenes.p: The wolf with a detective magnifying glass in a dark alley full of shady neon signs, coins being stolen by shadowy hands.

scenes.say: Red flag one: guaranteed returns. Nobody can guarantee crypto profits.
scenes.p: The wolf raises a big red flag in front of a shady man in a shiny suit opening a briefcase full of money.

scenes.say: Red flag two: giveaways. Send one coin, get two back. Always a scam, even with a famous face.
Red flag three: pressure. Act now, last chance. Real opportunities don't rush you.
Red flag four: a stranger who wants to teach you trading, then moves you to a special app.
If it sounds too good to be true, it is. Close the chat and block.
Follow for part sixteen: what a rug pull is, and how to avoid one. Not financial advice.

16.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part sixteen.

scenes.say: You buy a new coin, it's going up, and suddenly it's worth zero. That's a rug pull.
scenes.p: The wolf stands on a fancy rug that is being violently pulled out from under his feet, he flies in the air surprised.

scenes.say: The creators hype a token, attract buyers, then take all the money and disappear.
scenes.p: Shady masked developers run away through a back door carrying big sacks of gold coins, a party stage with fireworks left empty.

scenes.say: Warning sign one: an anonymous team, no track record, and huge promises.
Warning sign two: the developers hold a huge share of the supply.
Warning sign three: you can buy, but you can't sell. That's called a honeypot.
scenes.p: The wolf stuck inside a giant sticky honey pot, coins glued around him, annoyed face.

scenes.say: Stick to established coins, and treat brand new tokens as money you're ready to lose.
Follow for part seventeen: phishing, and the fake apps that empty wallets. Not financial advice.

17.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part seventeen.

scenes.say: One wrong click can drain your wallet in seconds.
scenes.p: The wolf's finger hovers over a glowing link on a laptop that has a hidden sharp fishing hook, dramatic tension.

scenes.say: Phishing means fake websites, emails or messages that look exactly like the real ones.
scenes.p: Two identical glowing websites side by side on big screens, one of them hides a fishing hook behind it, the wolf comparing them.

scenes.say: They ask you to log in, connect your wallet, or type your seed phrase. And then they take everything.
Always type the address yourself, or use a saved bookmark. Don't trust links in emails or ads.
Download wallet apps only from the official site or app store, and check who the developer is.
And never approve a wallet transaction you don't fully understand.
Follow for part eighteen: diversification, done the right way. Not financial advice.

18.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part eighteen.

scenes.say: Putting everything in one coin is risky. But owning fifty random coins isn't diversification either.
scenes.p: The wolf balances one wobbling basket with all the eggs, next to a messy overflowing basket with dozens of eggs falling out.

scenes.say: Diversification means spreading risk, so one bad bet can't sink your whole portfolio.
But most crypto moves together. When Bitcoin drops, many altcoins drop even harder.
So real diversification also means not having all your money in crypto.
scenes.p: The wolf at a table with separate piles: cash, gold bars, a small house model, and a small pile of crypto coins.

scenes.say: A few solid coins you actually understand beat a long list of random ones.
Follow for part nineteen: a simple way to build a crypto portfolio. Not financial advice.

19.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part nineteen.

scenes.say: Here's a simple way many investors structure a crypto portfolio: a core, and satellites.
scenes.p: The wolf in an astronaut suit floating in space next to a big golden planet with small moons orbiting it.

scenes.say: The core is the biggest part, usually the most established coins, like Bitcoin and Ethereum.
The satellites are small positions in riskier coins that could grow faster, or go to zero.
scenes.p: Small colorful moons orbiting the golden planet, one moon exploding into dust, the wolf watching from his spaceship.

scenes.say: Big core, small satellites. Never the other way round.
That way, if one risky bet fails, your core keeps you in the game.
And check it a few times a year, rebalancing if it gets out of shape.
Follow for part twenty: position sizing, the rule that keeps you alive. Not financial advice.

20.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty.

scenes.say: Picking the right coin matters less than how much money you put into it.
Position sizing means deciding how big each investment is, before you buy.
scenes.p: The wolf measures piles of gold coins with a big ruler like a tailor, careful.

scenes.say: A common rule for traders: risk only one or two percent of your account on a single trade.
That way, even ten losing trades in a row won't wipe you out.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a strong shield while ten small arrows bounce off it, standing firm and smiling.

scenes.say: Bigger bets feel exciting, but one bad move can undo months of gains.
Small, consistent positions are boring. And boring is how you stay in the game.
Follow for part twenty-one: the hidden fees eating your profits. Not financial advice.

21.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-one.

scenes.say: You might be losing money to fees without even noticing.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a bag of gold coins while tiny gremlins secretly nibble the coins from behind.

scenes.say: Trading fees: every time you buy or sell, the exchange takes a small cut.
scenes.p: The wolf drives a small car through a futuristic toll booth where a robotic arm takes a gold coin.

scenes.say: The spread: the gap between the buy price and the sell price. Instant buy buttons often hide a big one.
Network fees: moving coins on a blockchain costs a fee, and it changes with demand.
Withdrawal fees: some exchanges charge extra to send your coins out.
Small fees, repeated a hundred times, become big losses. Trade less, and compare more.
Follow for part twenty-two: the mistake that sends coins into the void forever. Not financial advice.

22.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-two.

scenes.say: Send crypto on the wrong network, and it can be gone forever.
scenes.p: A gold coin falling into a swirling black hole in space, the wolf reaching out in shock.

scenes.say: Many coins exist on several blockchains. USDT, for example, runs on Ethereum, Tron and others.
scenes.p: A gold coin standing at a junction of several glowing futuristic highways of different colors, the wolf pointing at the signs without text.

scenes.say: Sender and receiver must use the same network. If not, the money may never arrive.
Always double check the address: paste it, then compare the first and last characters.
Watch out for clipboard malware, which secretly swaps the address you pasted.
For big amounts, send a small test first. A small fee beats a big mistake.
Follow for part twenty-three: gas fees, and why they sometimes explode. Not financial advice.

23.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-three.

scenes.say: Ever tried to send crypto, and the fee was higher than the amount? Let's talk about gas.
scenes.p: The wolf stares in shock at a giant gas pump with a huge glowing price, holding a tiny coin.

scenes.say: On Ethereum, every action needs computing power. Gas is the fee you pay for it.
When the network is busy, fees go up. Like taxi prices at rush hour.
scenes.p: A massive traffic jam of yellow taxis at rush hour in a neon city, the wolf stuck in one taxi looking at the meter.

scenes.say: That's why layer two networks were built. They bundle many transactions together and settle them on Ethereum.
scenes.p: A big futuristic bus carrying many small coins onto a fast highway, the wolf as the bus driver.

scenes.say: The result: much lower fees, while still relying on Ethereum for security.
Just make sure your exchange and your wallet support the layer two you're using.
Follow for part twenty-four: Bitcoin dominance and altcoin season. Not financial advice.

24.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-four.

scenes.say: There's one chart that shows whether Bitcoin or the altcoins are in charge: Bitcoin dominance.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a giant glowing pie chart where one huge golden slice dominates.

scenes.say: Bitcoin dominance is Bitcoin's share of the total crypto market.
When it rises, money is flowing into Bitcoin, and altcoins often struggle.
When it falls, money moves into altcoins. Some people call that altcoin season.
scenes.p: Colorful cartoon coins having a wild party with fireworks and music, the wolf dancing with them.

scenes.say: But altcoin seasons are short and hard to predict, and many altcoins never recover afterwards.
So watch this chart, but never use it as your only signal.
Follow for part twenty-five: how to read a candlestick. Not financial advice.

25.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-five.

scenes.say: Every crypto chart is made of these little candles. Here's how to read one in thirty seconds.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a giant glowing green candlestick bar like a trophy, a trading chart in the background.

scenes.say: Each candle shows four prices: where it opened, where it closed, the highest point and the lowest.
scenes.p: The wolf points with a stick at a giant candlestick bar on a stage, like a teacher in front of a class.

scenes.say: Green means it closed higher than it opened. Red means it closed lower.
scenes.p: One giant green candle and one giant red candle standing on a stage under spotlights, the wolf between them.

scenes.say: The thick part is the body. The thin lines are the wicks: the extremes the price touched.
A long wick below means sellers pushed the price down, but buyers pushed it back up.
But one candle is just a clue, not a signal. Always look at the bigger picture.
Follow for part twenty-six: support and resistance, explained. Not financial advice.

26.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-six.

scenes.say: Most people draw these two lines wrong. Support and resistance.
scenes.p: The wolf stands between a glowing green floor below and a glowing red ceiling above, a price chart bouncing between them.

scenes.say: Support is a price zone where buyers keep stepping in. Like a floor the price bounces off.
scenes.p: A bouncing golden ball hitting a glowing green floor and bouncing back up, the wolf watching with a clipboard.

scenes.say: Resistance is a zone where sellers keep showing up. Like a ceiling the price hits its head on.
They're zones, not exact prices. Draw a thick band, not a thin line.
And when resistance finally breaks, it often turns into the new support.
scenes.p: The golden ball smashes through the red ceiling, which turns green and becomes the new floor, the wolf cheering.

scenes.say: But no level holds forever. Always have a plan if it breaks the wrong way.
Follow for part twenty-seven: how to spot a trend. Not financial advice.

27.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-seven.

scenes.say: Fighting the trend is one of the fastest ways to lose money.
scenes.p: The wolf tries to swim upstream against a powerful river current, exhausted.

scenes.say: In an uptrend, the price makes higher highs and higher lows. Like a staircase going up.
scenes.p: The wolf climbs a glowing golden staircase that zigzags upward into the sky.

scenes.say: In a downtrend, it's the opposite: lower highs and lower lows. A staircase going down.
And when it moves sideways between the same levels, that's a range. No clear trend.
A simple rule: in an uptrend, look for buys near the lows. Don't short a rocket.
Trends can change, so always use a stop loss in case you're wrong.
Follow for part twenty-eight: moving averages, made simple. Not financial advice.

28.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-eight.

scenes.say: Price charts look messy. Moving averages clean them up.
scenes.p: The wolf with a vacuum cleaner cleaning up a messy zigzag chart, leaving a smooth glowing line.

scenes.say: A moving average is the average price over the last few days, updated every day.
Two famous ones are the fifty-day and the two-hundred-day averages.
scenes.p: Two smooth glowing lines of different colors racing like snakes across a giant chart, the wolf as race commentator.

scenes.say: When the price is above the two-hundred-day average, the long-term trend is usually considered healthy.
When the fifty crosses above the two hundred, traders call it a golden cross. Below is a death cross.
But moving averages are slow. They confirm moves, they don't predict them.
Follow for part twenty-nine: the RSI indicator. Not financial advice.

29.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part twenty-nine.

scenes.say: This indicator tells you when the market might be running too hot. It's called the RSI.
scenes.p: The wolf looks at a giant glowing speedometer gauge with the needle in the red zone, steam coming out.

scenes.say: The RSI measures how strong recent moves were, on a scale from zero to one hundred.
Above seventy is usually called overbought. The price went up fast, maybe too fast.
scenes.p: A rocket overheating with flames and steam, the wolf holding a fire extinguisher.

scenes.say: Below thirty is called oversold. The price fell fast, maybe too fast.
But careful: in strong trends, the RSI can stay overbought or oversold for weeks.
Use it as a warning light, never as a buy or sell button on its own.
Follow for part thirty: why volume matters. Not financial advice.

30.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty.

scenes.say: A price move without volume is like a party with no guests.
scenes.p: The wolf alone at a big party with balloons and music, the room completely empty, awkward.

scenes.say: Volume is how much of a coin was traded in a period of time.
scenes.p: A busy futuristic marketplace full of people trading glowing coins, the wolf counting them.

scenes.say: When the price breaks out with high volume, a lot of people agree with the move.
When it breaks out on low volume, it's often a fake move that fades quickly.
Huge volume after a long drop can mean panic selling, and sometimes, the end of the fall.
Price tells you what happened. Volume tells you how much conviction was behind it.
Follow for part thirty-one: lump sum or DCA, which one wins? Not financial advice.

31.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-one.

scenes.say: You have money to invest. All at once, or a little at a time?
Investing all at once is called lump sum. If the price goes up after, you win the most.
scenes.p: The wolf throws a giant bag of money into a rocket that launches upward, cheering.

scenes.say: But if it drops right after, you feel every bit of that fall.
DCA means splitting it into equal parts and buying on a fixed schedule.
You might miss part of a rally, but you avoid going all in at the worst moment.
In volatile markets like crypto, many people pick DCA simply because it's easier to stick with.
scenes.p: The wolf sleeping peacefully on a hammock next to a slowly filling coin jar.

scenes.say: Follow for part thirty-two: staking, and how it really works. Not financial advice.

32.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-two.

scenes.say: Can your crypto earn more crypto while you sleep? That's the idea behind staking.
scenes.p: The wolf sleeps in bed while small gold coins pop out of a plant pot next to him.

scenes.say: Some blockchains, like Ethereum, use proof of stake. Validators lock up coins to help secure the network.
In return, they earn rewards in new coins. You can join through an exchange or a staking service.
scenes.p: Small gold coins grow on a tree, the wolf harvesting them into a basket.

scenes.say: But there are risks. Your coins may be locked for a while, and you can't sell quickly.
The coin's price can drop more than the rewards you earn.
And if you stake through a platform, you're trusting that platform with your coins.
Follow for part thirty-three: DeFi, finance without banks. Not financial advice.

33.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-three.

scenes.say: What if you could lend, borrow and trade without a bank? That's DeFi.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in a futuristic open-air bank with no walls and no bankers, glowing machines doing the work.

scenes.say: DeFi means decentralized finance: apps built on blockchains that run with smart contracts.
On a decentralized exchange, you swap coins directly from your own wallet.
scenes.p: The wolf swaps a gold coin for a silver coin through a glowing portal from his own wallet, no clerk in sight.

scenes.say: On lending apps, you can deposit coins to earn interest, or borrow against your crypto.
The risk: smart contracts can have bugs, and hacks have stolen billions over the years.
And there's no customer support to call if you make a mistake. Start small, and learn first.
Follow for part thirty-four: liquidity pools and impermanent loss. Not financial advice.

34.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-four.

scenes.say: Ever wondered where decentralized exchanges get their coins? From liquidity pools.
scenes.p: The wolf stands next to a big swimming pool filled with gold and silver coins instead of water.

scenes.say: A liquidity pool is a pot of two coins that traders swap against. Users like you fill it.
In return, you earn a share of the trading fees.
scenes.p: The wolf relaxes on an inflatable in the coin pool while small coins drop on him from above.

scenes.say: But there's a catch called impermanent loss. When one coin's price moves a lot, the pool rebalances.
You can end up with less value than if you had simply held both coins.
Fees can make up for it, or not. Understand the math before you jump in.
Follow for part thirty-five: the truth about meme coins. Not financial advice.

35.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-five.

scenes.say: Meme coins can go up a thousand percent. They can also go to zero by Friday.
scenes.p: The wolf watches a cartoon coin with a silly dog face shoot up like a rocket and then fall into a trash can.

scenes.say: A meme coin is a token driven by jokes, internet culture and hype, not by a product.
scenes.p: A colorful cartoon coin with a funny face wearing sunglasses on a stage, a crowd cheering with phones.

scenes.say: Prices move on social media posts, influencers and pure attention.
For every meme coin that made people rich, thousands went to almost zero.
scenes.p: A graveyard full of tiny tombstones shaped like coins with funny faces, the wolf walking through with a lantern.

scenes.say: Early insiders often sell to the latecomers. And the latecomers are usually us.
If you play, treat it like a lottery ticket. A tiny amount you can lose completely.
Follow for part thirty-six: presales, and why most of them go wrong. Not financial advice.

36.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-six.

scenes.say: Get in early before it lists! That's how presales are sold. Here's the catch.
scenes.p: A flashy salesman with a megaphone in front of a shiny gift box, the wolf raising an eyebrow.

scenes.say: In a presale, you buy tokens of a project before they're tradable on exchanges.
Often your tokens are locked for months, and you can't sell even if things go wrong.
Early investors and the team often bought cheaper than you, and they may sell the moment it lists.
Many presales are pure marketing, and some are straight-up scams that never deliver a token.
scenes.p: The wolf opens the mystery box and finds it completely empty except for a little cloud of dust.

scenes.say: Check the team, the token unlock schedule, and assume you could lose it all.
Follow for part thirty-seven: free crypto airdrops, real or scam? Not financial advice.

37.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part thirty-seven.

scenes.say: Free crypto falling from the sky? Sometimes it's real. Often it's a trap.
scenes.p: Gold coins falling from the sky with little parachutes, the wolf looking up suspiciously.

scenes.say: An airdrop is when a project gives away tokens, usually to early users of its app or network.
Real airdrops never ask you to send money or share your seed phrase.
Scam airdrops put random tokens in your wallet, then lead you to a fake site to claim them.
Connect your wallet there and approve, and it can be drained in one click.
If you didn't expect it, don't touch it. Unknown tokens are best ignored.
scenes.p: The wolf walks away calmly ignoring a glowing suspicious coin on the ground.

scenes.say: Follow for part thirty-eight: how to read a crypto whitepaper. Not financial advice.

38.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 38.

scenes.say: Before you buy any coin, skim one document: the whitepaper.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a thick glowing document scroll and reads it seriously in a grand library full of tall bookshelves.

scenes.say: It's the project's official plan: the problem it solves, how it works, and how the token is used.
First: does this project really need a blockchain, or is the token just there to raise money?
scenes.p: The wolf scratches his head looking at a strange complicated machine full of gears that does nothing useful, a shiny coin sitting on top of it.

scenes.say: Second, look for specifics. Real numbers, real timelines, real people. Vague buzzwords are a red flag.
Third, check the token section: how many coins exist, and who gets them.
Copied text, impossible promises, or no whitepaper at all? Walk away.
Follow for part 39: tokenomics, and why supply matters. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: Close-up of the wolf pointing at the viewer with a confident grin, on a skyscraper rooftop at night, city lights below.

39.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 39.

scenes.say: Two coins can have the same great technology and completely different results. The difference is often tokenomics.
scenes.p: The wolf compares two identical robots: one stands on a small neat pile of coins, the other is buried under an overflowing avalanche of coins.

scenes.say: Tokenomics means the economics of a token: how many exist, how new ones are created, and who holds them.
If new tokens are printed nonstop, your share keeps getting smaller. Like a pizza cut into more and more slices.
scenes.p: The wolf looks sadly at a pizza being cut into more and more tiny slices by a machine.

scenes.say: If a few wallets hold most of the supply, they can move the price whenever they want.
So look for a clear supply schedule, a fair distribution, and a real reason to hold the token.
Follow for part 40: what a stock really is. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf winks and gives a thumbs up to the viewer, modern office with big windows and a city view, sunny day.

scenes.say: When you buy a stock, you're not buying a piece of paper. You're buying a tiny piece of a real company.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a tiny glowing slice of a big modern company headquarters like a slice of cake, a stock exchange street behind him.

scenes.say: If the company grows and earns more, your piece can become worth more.
Some companies also share part of their profits with you. Those payments are called dividends.
But if the company struggles, the price can fall, and in the worst case, go to zero.
That's why investors study the business behind the stock, not just the price chart.
scenes.p: The wolf tours a busy factory floor with a clipboard, workers and machines all around him.

scenes.say: Follow for part 41: token unlocks, the hidden selling pressure. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf leans toward the viewer pointing with both index fingers, gold coins raining in the background, excited grin.

41.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 41.

scenes.say: A coin can drop even when the news is great. One hidden reason: token unlocks.
Many projects give tokens to the team and early investors, but lock them for months or years.
scenes.p: A giant glass safe full of gold coins locked with a big timer clock on its door, a group of people in suits waiting outside.

scenes.say: When those tokens unlock, a flood of new coins can hit the market at once.
scenes.p: The timer safe bursts open and a flood of gold coins pours into the street, the wolf running away from the wave.

scenes.say: Early investors often bought very cheap. Many take profit, and that selling can push the price down.
Before you buy, check the unlock schedule. Big unlocks coming soon mean extra risk.
Follow for part 42: fully diluted valuation, explained. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf in a podcast studio with a big microphone points at the viewer, neon lights, confident smile.

42.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 42.

scenes.say: A coin with a small market cap might not be as cheap as it looks. Meet fully diluted valuation.
Market cap counts only the coins in circulation today. Fully diluted valuation counts every coin that will ever exist.
scenes.p: The wolf looks at a small pile of coins on a table while a gigantic hidden mountain of coins looms behind a theater curtain.

scenes.say: If only ten percent of the coins are circulating, the FDV can be ten times the market cap.
And as the rest unlocks, the price has to absorb all those new coins.
So compare both numbers. A huge gap means a lot of future supply is coming.
Follow for part 43: how the stock market works. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf stands on a balcony above a classic stock exchange street with columns and flags, pointing at the viewer.

scenes.say: The stock market sounds complicated. It's really just a giant marketplace.
scenes.p: A huge classic stock exchange hall with marble columns, traders and big glowing screens, the wolf standing in the middle in awe.

scenes.say: Companies sell shares to raise money. Then investors buy and sell those shares with each other.
Prices move with supply and demand. More buyers than sellers, the price rises. More sellers, it falls.
The New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq are where most big American stocks trade.
Today you can buy shares from an app in seconds, through a broker.
And unlike crypto, most stock markets close at night and on weekends.
scenes.p: The wolf locks the big doors of a classic stock exchange building at night under the moon, holding a lantern.

scenes.say: Follow for part 44: circulating, total and max supply. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf sits on a big stack of gold bars and points at the viewer with a relaxed grin, luxury vault background.

44.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 44.

scenes.say: Every coin has three supply numbers, and most people mix them up.
Circulating supply: the coins that exist and can be traded right now.
Total supply: all the coins created so far, including the ones still locked.
Max supply: the hard limit that can ever exist. For Bitcoin, it's twenty-one million.
Some coins have no max supply at all. Not always bad, but you need to know how fast new coins appear.
Follow for part 45: how to research a coin in five minutes. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf on a busy trading floor full of screens points at the viewer with a confident smile.

45.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 45.

scenes.say: Here's a five-minute checklist before buying any coin.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a big clipboard with a checklist and a stopwatch, ready and focused, office background.

scenes.say: One: what does it actually do? If you can't explain it in one sentence, that's a warning.
Two: check the market cap, the FDV and the unlock schedule.
Three: who's behind it? A known team and a real track record matter.
Four: is there real trading volume on reputable exchanges?
Five: search the name plus the word scam. Five minutes now can save you a lot of money.
Follow for part 46: what an index like the S&P 500 is. Not financial advice.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a smartphone toward the viewer with a big glowing heart icon on the screen, smiling, neon city at night.

scenes.say: When people say the market is up today, they usually mean an index, like the S&P 500.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a giant glowing scoreboard made of hundreds of small colorful tiles, inside a stock exchange hall.

scenes.say: The S&P 500 tracks about five hundred of the largest companies in the United States.
Instead of following one company, it shows how the big US market is doing overall.
Historically, it has gone up over the long run, but with big crashes along the way.
You can't buy the index itself, but you can buy funds that copy it.
Follow for part 47: the crypto slang you need to know. Not financial advice.

47.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 47.

scenes.say: Crypto has its own language. Here's what people are actually saying.
scenes.p: The wolf reads a big old dictionary book with glowing emoji symbols flying out of the pages, library background.

scenes.say: HODL means holding for the long term, no matter what. It started as a typo of hold, back in 2013.
FOMO is the fear of missing out. FUD is fear, uncertainty and doubt.
A whale is someone holding a huge amount. Rekt means you lost big.
scenes.p: A gigantic cartoon whale made of gold coins swims through the sky above the city, the wolf looking up amazed.

scenes.say: To the moon means people expect the price to skyrocket. Usually, that's exactly when to be careful.
And DYOR means do your own research. Good advice, always.
Follow for part 48: market orders versus limit orders. Not financial advice.

48.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 48.

scenes.say: When you buy crypto, the button you press can change the price you pay.
A market order buys immediately, at the best price available right now. Fast, but you accept whatever price is there.
scenes.p: The wolf grabs a coin in a hurry from a fast moving conveyor belt at a busy market stall.

scenes.say: A limit order lets you choose your price. It only fills if the market reaches it.
scenes.p: The wolf sits patiently fishing on a wooden pier, a gold coin slowly swimming toward his hook.

scenes.say: Limit orders often have lower fees, and they protect you from sudden price jumps.
But if the price never comes, your order never fills.
Follow for part 49: ETFs, explained. Not financial advice.
Want to own five hundred companies with one click? That's what an ETF can do.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a big transparent basket filled with tiny glowing company buildings, smiling.

scenes.say: An ETF is a fund that trades on the stock exchange, just like a single stock.
Inside, it holds a basket of assets: stocks, bonds, gold, or even Bitcoin.
Index ETFs are cheap to own, because they simply copy an index.
The big advantage: instant diversification. The big rule: always check the fees.
Follow for part 50: slippage, and how to avoid it. Not financial advice.

50.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 50.

scenes.say: You clicked buy at one price, but you paid more. That's slippage.
scenes.p: The wolf slips on a banana peel while carrying a gold coin, the coin flying out of his paws, comic style, city street.

scenes.say: Slippage is the difference between the price you expect and the price you actually get.
It happens when the price moves fast, or when there aren't enough buyers and sellers at your price.
Small coins with low liquidity can have huge slippage, especially on decentralized exchanges.
The fixes: use limit orders, trade liquid pairs, and split big orders into smaller ones.
Follow for part 51: the order book, explained simply. Not financial advice.

51.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 51.

scenes.say: Every exchange keeps a live list of who wants to buy and who wants to sell. It's called the order book.
scenes.p: The wolf reads a giant glowing ledger book with green entries on the left page and red entries on the right page, futuristic hall.

scenes.say: On one side, the bids: buyers, and the prices they're willing to pay.
On the other side, the asks: sellers, and the prices they want.
The gap between the best bid and the best ask is called the spread.
A thick order book means you can trade big amounts without moving the price much.
Follow for part 52: index funds and Warren Buffett's famous bet. Not financial advice.
In 2008, Warren Buffett made a ten-year bet: a simple S&P 500 index fund against hedge funds picked by professionals.
scenes.p: A wise old investor with glasses shakes hands with a group of sharp fund managers over a huge golden trophy, the wolf watching, cartoon style.

scenes.say: The professionals charged high fees and tried to beat the market.
The index fund simply held the whole market, with tiny fees.
After ten years, the index fund won, by a wide margin.
The lesson: low costs and patience often beat clever stock picking.
Follow for part 53: centralized versus decentralized exchanges. Not financial advice.

53.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 53.

scenes.say: There are two kinds of crypto exchanges, and they work very differently.
A centralized exchange is a company. It holds your coins, matches orders, and usually has customer support.
It's easier for beginners, but you're trusting that company with your money.
A decentralized exchange is a set of smart contracts. You trade directly from your own wallet.
More control, but no help desk, and you're responsible for every click.
Follow for part 54: why exchanges ask for your ID. Not financial advice.

54.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 54.

scenes.say: Why does a crypto app want a photo of your passport?
scenes.p: The wolf holds up his passport next to his face while a smartphone camera scans him, slightly annoyed.

scenes.say: It's called KYC: know your customer. Regulated exchanges must verify who their users are.
It's there to fight money laundering, fraud, and stolen funds.
The downside: your data is stored by the company, so choose exchanges with a strong security record.
And be careful: real exchanges ask for ID inside their official app, never through a random link or chat.
Follow for part 55: dividends, explained. Not financial advice.
Some stocks pay you just for holding them. Those payments are called dividends.
A company makes a profit and sends part of it to its shareholders, often every three months.
scenes.p: The wolf opens his mailbox and finds an envelope full of gold coins, happy, sunny suburban street.

scenes.say: The dividend yield is the yearly dividend divided by the stock price.
Mature companies, like utilities or big consumer brands, often pay steady dividends.
But a very high yield can be a warning sign. Sometimes it's high only because the price crashed.
Follow for part 56: proof of reserves. Not financial advice.

56.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 56.

scenes.say: After FTX, a big question: does your exchange actually have your money?
Proof of reserves is a way for an exchange to show it holds enough assets to cover customer balances.
Usually, it publishes wallet addresses and a cryptographic check of user balances.
But it's only a snapshot. It may not show all the debts the exchange owes.
scenes.p: The wolf takes a photo of a neat vault with an old camera, while behind the vault wall a giant pile of unpaid bills is hidden.

scenes.say: It's a good sign, not a guarantee. Don't keep more on an exchange than you need.
Follow for part 57: the Mt. Gox story. Not financial advice.

57.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 57.

scenes.say: In 2014, the biggest Bitcoin exchange in the world collapsed. Its name was Mt. Gox.
At its peak, it handled most of the world's Bitcoin trading.
Then it announced that around eight hundred fifty thousand bitcoin were missing, lost to hackers and mismanagement.
scenes.p: An empty giant vault with a broken door, dust and a few scattered coins on the floor, the wolf standing inside with a flashlight, shocked.

scenes.say: Customers waited about ten years before repayments finally began.
The lesson crypto keeps teaching: not your keys, not your coins.
Follow for part 58: reinvesting dividends. Not financial advice.
What you do with your dividends can matter more than the dividends themselves.
Instead of spending them, you can use them to buy more shares, automatically.
More shares pay more dividends, which buy even more shares. That's compounding.
scenes.p: A snowball made of gold coins rolls down a snowy hill growing bigger and bigger, the wolf running beside it cheering.

scenes.say: Over decades, reinvested dividends have made up a big part of total stock market returns.
Many brokers offer a DRIP, a dividend reinvestment plan, often with no extra fees.
Follow for part 59: custodial versus non-custodial wallets. Not financial advice.

59.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 59.

scenes.say: Who really holds your crypto? The answer decides who's in control.
With a custodial wallet, a company holds your keys. Like a bank account: easy, but they control access.
With a non-custodial wallet, only you hold the keys. Full control, and full responsibility.
If the company freezes withdrawals or goes bust, custodial users can lose access.
Lose your seed phrase in a non-custodial wallet, and nobody can help you.
Follow for part 60: what a block really is. Not financial advice.

60.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 60.

scenes.say: Everyone talks about the blockchain. But what is a block, really?
scenes.p: The wolf holds a glowing transparent cube filled with tiny paper receipts, examining it curiously.

scenes.say: A block is a bundle of transactions. Like a page in a giant shared notebook.
Each block contains a fingerprint of the previous one. That's what links them into a chain.
Change one old transaction, and every block after it breaks. That's why history is so hard to rewrite.
On Bitcoin, a new block is added about every ten minutes.
Follow for part 61: the P/E ratio. Not financial advice.
Is a stock expensive or cheap? One quick number gives a first clue: the P/E ratio.
P/E means price to earnings: the share price divided by the profit per share.
A P/E of twenty means investors pay twenty dollars for every dollar of yearly profit.
scenes.p: The wolf at a shop counter pays a tall stack of gold coins to buy one single small gold coin, thinking hard.

scenes.say: Fast-growing companies often have high P/Es. Slow, mature ones usually have lower ones.
Compare P/Es within the same industry, and never use it as your only reason to buy.
Follow for part 62: hashing, explained simply. Not financial advice.

62.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 62.

scenes.say: Blockchains rely on a kind of digital fingerprint, called a hash.
scenes.p: The wolf looks through a big magnifying glass at a giant glowing fingerprint made of light, futuristic lab.

scenes.say: A hash function turns any data into a fixed-length code. Same input, same code, every time.
Change even one letter, and the code changes completely.
And you can't run it backwards. From the code, you can't recover the original data.
That's how blocks are linked together, and how Bitcoin mining works.
Follow for part 63: public and private keys. Not financial advice.

63.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 63.

scenes.say: Your crypto wallet runs on two keys. Mix them up, and you could lose everything.
The public key is like your email address. You can share it, so people can send you coins.
scenes.p: The wolf hands out business cards with a glowing blue key symbol to friendly people, smiling.

scenes.say: The private key is like the password to that email. Whoever has it controls your funds.
Your seed phrase is a human-readable backup of your private keys.
Share the public one freely. Never, ever share the private one.
Follow for part 64: revenue versus profit. Not financial advice.
A company can sell billions and still lose money. Here's why.
scenes.p: A huge river of gold coins flows into a company building while most of the coins leak out of holes in the back wall, the wolf watching worried.

scenes.say: Revenue is all the money that comes in from sales.
Profit is what's left after paying for everything: staff, materials, rent, taxes and interest.
A fast-growing company may have huge revenue and no profit yet, because it's investing to grow.
Healthy businesses eventually turn revenue into real, growing profit. That's what investors watch.
Follow for part 65: what a wallet address really is. Not financial advice.

65.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 65.

scenes.say: That long string of letters and numbers is your wallet address. Here's what it really is.
scenes.p: The wolf stands next to a futuristic glowing mailbox engraved with a very long code, holding a gold coin like a letter.

scenes.say: It's derived from your public key, and it's where people send you crypto.
Each blockchain has its own address format. A Bitcoin address is not an Ethereum address.
Anyone can see the balance and history of an address on the blockchain. It's public.
Always double-check the first and last characters before you send.
Follow for part 66: confirmations, and why transfers take time. Not financial advice.

66.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 66.

scenes.say: You sent crypto, and it still says pending. Why does it take time?
A transaction becomes real when it's included in a block. That's the first confirmation.
Each new block added on top is another confirmation, and makes reversing it harder.
scenes.p: The wolf stacks glowing transparent cubes one on top of another into a tall, stable tower.

scenes.say: That's why exchanges often wait for several confirmations before crediting your deposit.
And when the network is busy, paying a higher fee can get you into a block faster.
Follow for part 67: earnings reports. Not financial advice.
Four times a year, companies reveal their results, and the stock can jump or crash overnight.
scenes.p: The wolf stands at a podium on a stage presenting a big glowing report while a crowd of investors holds its breath.

scenes.say: An earnings report shows revenue, profit, and what the company expects for the future.
The stock reacts to the numbers versus expectations, not just to whether they're good or bad.
Great results can still sink a stock if investors expected even more.
So if you hold a stock, know its earnings dates. Volatility often spikes around them.
Follow for part 68: proof of work, explained. Not financial advice.

68.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 68.

scenes.say: Bitcoin is secured by computers playing a giant guessing game. It's called proof of work.
Miners race to find a special number that gives the block a hash below a target.
scenes.p: Rows of glowing mining machines in a huge warehouse, fans spinning, the wolf walking between them with a clipboard.

scenes.say: Finding it takes enormous computing power, but anyone can check the answer instantly.
The winner adds the next block and earns new bitcoin, plus the transaction fees.
To attack the network, you'd need more computing power than all the honest miners combined.
Follow for part 69: proof of work versus proof of stake. Not financial advice.

69.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 69.

scenes.say: There are two main ways to secure a blockchain: proof of work, and proof of stake.
scenes.p: The wolf stands between a noisy industrial mining machine on the left and a calm glowing vault of locked coins on the right.

scenes.say: Proof of work uses energy and machines. Security comes from the cost of computing.
Proof of stake uses locked coins. Validators put their own money at risk to verify blocks.
Cheat in proof of stake, and you can lose part of your stake. It's called slashing.
Bitcoin uses proof of work. Ethereum switched to proof of stake in 2022.
Follow for part 70: growth stocks versus value stocks. Not financial advice.
There are two classic styles of stock investing: growth, and value.
Growth stocks are companies expanding fast. Investors pay high prices for future potential.
Value stocks look cheap compared to their profits or assets. Often boring, sometimes overlooked.
scenes.p: The wolf finds a dusty treasure chest full of gold in a quiet old antique shop that everyone else ignores.

scenes.say: Growth can win big in good times, but falls hard when expectations drop.
Value can lag for years, then shine. Many investors simply own some of both.
Follow for part 71: soft forks and hard forks. Not financial advice.

71.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 71.

scenes.say: Sometimes a blockchain splits in two. It's called a fork.
scenes.p: A glowing chain of cubes splits into two separate branches like a fork in a road, the wolf standing at the split point.

scenes.say: A soft fork is a backward-compatible upgrade. Old software still works with the new rules.
A hard fork changes the rules in a way old software can't follow. If people disagree, you get two chains.
That's how Bitcoin Cash was born in 2017, splitting away from Bitcoin.
If you held coins before a split, you usually ended up with coins on both chains.
Follow for part 72: who is Satoshi Nakamoto. Not financial advice.

72.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 72.

scenes.say: Bitcoin's creator is still a mystery. The name: Satoshi Nakamoto.
scenes.p: A mysterious hooded figure with no visible face stands in the fog holding a glowing golden Bitcoin, the wolf watching from a distance.

scenes.say: In 2008, Satoshi published the Bitcoin whitepaper, and in early 2009, launched the network.
Satoshi worked with early developers online, then disappeared around 2011.
The coins believed to be Satoshi's, estimated at around one million bitcoin, have never moved.
No leader, no CEO, no company. Maybe that's exactly the point.
Follow for part 73: blue chip stocks. Not financial advice.
Blue chip stocks are the giants: big, established companies with long track records.
scenes.p: The wolf stands among towering skyscrapers of grand corporate headquarters, looking up, sunny day.

scenes.say: The name comes from poker, where the blue chips had the highest value.
scenes.p: The wolf at a poker table stacking shiny blue poker chips, warm casino lights.

scenes.say: They usually have strong brands, steady profits, and often pay dividends.
They're generally less volatile than small companies, but not risk-free. Giants can fall too.
Many investors use them as the solid core of a portfolio.
Follow for part 74: the genesis block. Not financial advice.

74.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 74.

scenes.say: On January 3rd, 2009, the very first Bitcoin block was created. It's called the genesis block.
scenes.p: A single glowing golden cube floating alone in deep darkness like the first star of the universe, the wolf gazing at it in wonder.

scenes.say: Satoshi hid a message inside it: a newspaper headline about banks getting a second bailout.
scenes.p: The wolf reads an old newspaper with a dramatic front page on a park bench in London, foggy morning.

scenes.say: Many see it as a statement: Bitcoin was born as an answer to the 2008 financial crisis.
And the fifty bitcoin reward in that block can never be spent.
Every Bitcoin block since then links back, one by one, to that very first block.
Follow for part 75: Bitcoin Pizza Day. Not financial advice.

75.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 75.

scenes.say: On May 22nd, 2010, a programmer paid ten thousand bitcoin for two pizzas.
scenes.p: The wolf happily holds two large pizza boxes while handing over a huge sack of golden Bitcoin coins, retro kitchen.

scenes.say: It was one of the first real purchases ever made with Bitcoin.
At today's prices, those pizzas would be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, or even more.
But without people willing to spend it, Bitcoin might never have become real money.
Today, May 22nd is celebrated every year as Bitcoin Pizza Day.
Follow for part 76: the danger of penny stocks. Not financial advice.
A stock for under a dollar sounds like a bargain. Usually, it's a trap.
Penny stocks are shares of tiny companies, often under five dollars, sometimes traded outside the major exchanges.
scenes.p: A shady back-alley market stall selling cheap glowing stock certificates from a bargain bin, the wolf frowning.

scenes.say: They come with little information, low trading volume, and huge price swings.
That makes them perfect for pump and dump schemes.
A low price doesn't mean cheap. Look at the business, not the price tag.
Follow for part 77: satoshis: you don't need a whole bitcoin. Not financial advice.

77.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 77.

scenes.say: You don't need to buy a whole bitcoin. Most people never do.
One bitcoin can be split into one hundred million smaller units, called satoshis, or sats.
scenes.p: The wolf slices a giant golden Bitcoin into a cloud of countless tiny glowing coins with a laser, amazed.

scenes.say: Most exchanges let you start with just a few dollars.
Stacking sats simply means buying small amounts, regularly.
What matters is the percentage you gain or lose, not whether you own a whole coin.
Follow for part 78: the Lightning Network. Not financial advice.

78.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 78.

scenes.say: Bitcoin can be slow and expensive for small payments. The Lightning Network is the fix.
scenes.p: The wolf rides a glowing golden lightning bolt across a night city, sparkling coins trailing behind him.

scenes.say: Lightning is a second layer built on top of Bitcoin.
Two people open a payment channel, then send many payments instantly, almost for free.
Only the opening and the closing get recorded on the main blockchain.
It's made for small, fast payments, like buying a coffee.
scenes.p: The wolf pays for a coffee at a cozy cafe by tapping his phone on a reader, a tiny lightning bolt sparkling, the barista smiling.

scenes.say: Follow for part 79: stock splits. Not financial advice.
A stock split makes each share cheaper, but it doesn't make you any richer.
In a four-for-one split, one share becomes four, each worth a quarter of the price.
Apple did exactly that in 2020. Nvidia did a ten-for-one split in 2024.
The company's total value stays the same. Only the number of shares changes.
Splits can make shares easier to buy and bring attention, but they don't change the business.
Follow for part 80: Bitcoin ETFs. Not financial advice.

80.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 80.

scenes.say: In January 2024, the United States approved spot Bitcoin ETFs. That was huge.
scenes.p: The wolf rings a big golden bell on a stock exchange balcony while confetti and golden Bitcoin coins fly, a crowd cheering below.

scenes.say: A Bitcoin ETF gives you Bitcoin exposure through a normal brokerage account.
The fund holds the bitcoin. You hold shares of the fund.
It's simple and familiar, but you pay a yearly fee, and you don't hold your own keys.
For big institutions, it opened a regulated door into Bitcoin.
Follow for part 81: Ethereum ETFs. Not financial advice.

81.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 81.

scenes.say: After Bitcoin, Ethereum got its turn. Spot Ethereum ETFs started trading in the US in July 2024.
They work the same way: a fund holds ether, and you buy shares of the fund.
It's a way to follow ether's price without managing a wallet.
One difference: at launch, the US funds didn't include staking rewards.
Same rules apply: check the fees, and know exactly what you're buying.
Follow for part 82: share buybacks. Not financial advice.
Sometimes a company buys back its own shares. It's called a buyback.
scenes.p: The wolf in a suit buys back golden stock certificates from a line of people at a counter, smiling.

scenes.say: Fewer shares remain, so each one owns a slightly bigger piece of the company.
It's another way to return money to shareholders, besides dividends.
Apple, for example, has spent hundreds of billions of dollars on buybacks over the years.
But buybacks at very high prices, or paid for with debt, can destroy value.
Follow for part 83: coins versus tokens. Not financial advice.

83.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 83.

scenes.say: Coin or token? People use the words as if they're the same, but they're not.
A coin is native to its own blockchain. Bitcoin on Bitcoin, ether on Ethereum.
A token is built on top of another blockchain, using smart contracts.
Stablecoins, meme coins and most app tokens are actually tokens.
Why it matters: a token depends on the security of the chain it lives on.
Follow for part 84: ERC-20 tokens. Not financial advice.

84.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 84.

scenes.say: Thousands of tokens live on Ethereum, and most follow the same standard: ERC-20.
scenes.p: The wolf inspects a futuristic factory where identical tokens in many colors roll off a conveyor belt, quality control.

scenes.say: It's a shared set of rules, so every wallet and exchange knows how to handle the token.
That's why you can hold USDT, LINK or UNI in the same Ethereum wallet.
But anyone can create an ERC-20 token in minutes. A standard doesn't mean it's safe.
Always verify the official contract address before buying a token.
Follow for part 85: IPOs. Not financial advice.
When a private company sells shares to the public for the first time, that's an IPO.
It raises money for the company, and lets early investors cash out.
IPO prices can jump on day one, then slide for months after the hype.
Small investors often get in only after the big first-day jump.
scenes.p: The wolf arrives late at a party where the confetti is already on the floor and the cake is almost gone.

scenes.say: Many investors wait for a few earnings reports before buying a new IPO.
Follow for part 86: NFTs, honestly explained. Not financial advice.

86.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 86.

scenes.say: NFTs made headlines with crazy prices. Here's what they really are.
scenes.p: The wolf in a modern art gallery looks puzzled at a framed glowing cartoon monkey picture with a huge price tag hanging below it.

scenes.say: An NFT is a unique token on a blockchain that proves ownership of something digital, like art or an in-game item.
Fungible means interchangeable, like dollars. Non-fungible means one of a kind.
In 2021, some sold for millions. Then most collections lost almost all their value.
Owning an NFT usually doesn't mean owning the copyright. And its price depends purely on demand.
Follow for part 87: oracles: how blockchains see the real world. Not financial advice.

87.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 87.

scenes.say: Blockchains can't see the outside world. They don't know the price of gold, or who won the game.
scenes.p: A big friendly blockchain robot wearing a blindfold sits in a room, the wolf waving his paw in front of its face.

scenes.say: An oracle brings real-world data onto the blockchain, so smart contracts can use it.
scenes.p: A glowing messenger owl carries data scrolls from a busy city into a futuristic blockchain tower, the wolf watching.

scenes.say: Lending apps use price oracles to know when to liquidate a loan.
If an oracle reports a wrong price, a whole protocol can break. That's why data from many sources is combined.
Chainlink is the best-known oracle network.
Follow for part 88: the Magnificent Seven. Not financial advice.
Seven companies have carried a huge part of the US stock market. They're called the Magnificent Seven.
scenes.p: Seven giant futuristic glowing skyscrapers standing in a row over a city skyline, the wolf on a hill looking at them.

scenes.say: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla.
Together, they make up around a third of the S&P 500's total value.
When they rise, the whole index looks great. When they fall, they drag everything down.
If you own an S&P 500 fund, you already own a lot of them. Know your concentration.
Follow for part 89: bridges, and why they get hacked. Not financial advice.

89.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 89.

scenes.say: Some of the biggest hacks in crypto history didn't hit exchanges. They hit bridges.
scenes.p: A glowing futuristic bridge between two floating islands collapses in the middle, gold coins falling into the abyss, the wolf shocked.

scenes.say: A bridge moves tokens between blockchains, by locking them on one side and issuing copies on the other.
All those locked funds make bridges a giant target.
In 2022, the Ronin bridge lost about six hundred million dollars in a single attack.
Use bridges only when you need them, stick to well-known ones, and don't leave funds sitting inside.
Follow for part 90: layer one versus layer two. Not financial advice.

90.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 90.

scenes.say: Layer one, layer two. What's the difference?
scenes.p: A two-level futuristic highway: a big solid road at the bottom and a fast glowing express lane above it, the wolf driving on the upper level.

scenes.say: A layer one is the base blockchain itself, like Bitcoin, Ethereum or Solana.
A layer two is built on top of it, to make transactions faster and cheaper.
It processes many transactions off the main chain, then settles them on layer one.
Lightning is a Bitcoin layer two. Arbitrum, Optimism and Base are Ethereum layer twos.
Follow for part 91: Apple: from near bankruptcy to giant. Not financial advice.
In 1997, Apple was close to bankruptcy.
scenes.p: A sad, almost empty computer shop with dusty shelves and an apple-shaped sign, rain outside, the wolf looking in through the window.

scenes.say: Steve Jobs came back, cut the product line, and Microsoft invested one hundred fifty million dollars.
Then came the iMac, the iPod, and in 2007, the iPhone.
scenes.p: The wolf on a big stage holds up a sleek glowing smartphone to a cheering audience under spotlights.

scenes.say: In 2018, Apple became the first US company worth a trillion dollars.
The lesson: companies can change completely. Look at where a business is going, not only where it's been.
Follow for part 92: the three types of stablecoins. Not financial advice.

92.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 92.

scenes.say: Not all stablecoins are built the same. There are three main types.
Fiat-backed, like USDT and USDC: backed by cash and government bonds held by a company.
Crypto-backed, like DAI: backed by more crypto than the stablecoins issued, locked in smart contracts.
scenes.p: The wolf pours a big pile of gold coins into a glowing machine that gives back a smaller neat stack of green dollar coins.

scenes.say: Algorithmic: kept stable only by code and incentives. TerraUSD was one, and it collapsed in 2022.
The more transparent the backing, the more trust a stablecoin deserves.
Follow for part 93: what a depeg is. Not financial advice.

93.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 93.

scenes.say: A stablecoin is supposed to stay at one dollar. When it doesn't, that's a depeg.
