scenes.p: A green dollar coin wobbles and slides down off a balance pedestal, the wolf reaching out to catch it.

scenes.say: In March 2023, USDC briefly fell to around eighty-seven cents.
Its issuer had billions of dollars stuck in a bank that had just collapsed.
It recovered within days, once those funds were safe. TerraUSD never did.
The lesson: even stablecoins carry risk. Spread out, and watch the news.
Follow for part 94: the Nvidia and chips story. Not financial advice.
A company that made graphics chips for video games became one of the most valuable on Earth.
scenes.p: A glowing computer chip as big as a skyscraper rises out of a city like a monument, the wolf looking up at it.

scenes.say: Nvidia was founded in 1993. Its chips were built to draw game graphics, fast.
scenes.p: The wolf plays a retro video game at an arcade machine with colorful graphics, excited.

scenes.say: It turned out the same chips were perfect for training artificial intelligence.
When AI exploded, demand exploded too. In 2025, Nvidia became the first company ever worth four trillion dollars.
But high expectations mean big swings. Even giants can drop thirty percent in a few weeks.
Follow for part 95: Solana in sixty seconds. Not financial advice.

95.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 95.

scenes.say: Solana, in sixty seconds.
scenes.p: The wolf races on a sleek purple and teal futuristic motorbike through a neon tunnel at high speed.

scenes.say: Solana is a layer one blockchain launched in 2020, built for speed and very low fees.
It's popular for trading, payments and, yes, meme coins.
It had several network outages in its early years, and lost over ninety percent of its value in the 2022 crash.
It came back strongly, but it shows how volatile even big altcoins can be.
Follow for part 96: XRP in sixty seconds. Not financial advice.

96.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 96.

scenes.say: XRP, in sixty seconds.
scenes.p: The wolf at a futuristic money transfer terminal sends glowing coins across a giant world map instantly.

scenes.say: XRP was created in 2012 by the founders of Ripple, a company focused on cross-border payments.
Its transactions settle in seconds, and cost a tiny fraction of a cent.
From 2020, Ripple fought a long legal battle with the US SEC, which shook the price for years.
scenes.p: The wolf in a courtroom watches a dramatic trial, a judge with a gavel and lawyers arguing, tense atmosphere.

scenes.say: A big part of the supply is held by Ripple itself. Know that before you invest.
Follow for part 97: Coca-Cola and the power of boring companies. Not financial advice.
One of Warren Buffett's most famous investments isn't tech. It's soda.
scenes.p: The wolf sits at a vintage diner counter with a classic red soda bottle, relaxed, 1950s style.

scenes.say: Berkshire Hathaway began buying Coca-Cola shares in 1988, and still holds them today.
Coca-Cola has raised its dividend every year for more than sixty years.
A simple product, a global brand, and steady demand. Boring, but powerful.
Exciting stocks get the headlines. Boring ones often quietly compound.
Follow for part 98: Cardano in sixty seconds. Not financial advice.

98.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 98.

scenes.say: Cardano, in sixty seconds.
scenes.p: The wolf wears a white lab coat over his suit and examines a glowing blue blockchain model through a microscope, science lab.

scenes.say: Cardano launched in 2017. It was founded by Charles Hoskinson, one of Ethereum's co-founders.
Its approach is slow and research-driven, with upgrades based on peer-reviewed papers.
It uses proof of stake, and smart contracts only arrived in 2021.
Critics say it moves too slowly. Fans say that's the point. Either way, it's still a volatile asset.
Follow for part 99: Dogecoin, the joke that became a giant. Not financial advice.

99.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 99.

scenes.say: A coin made as a joke became one of the biggest cryptos in the world.
scenes.p: A cheerful cartoon Shiba Inu dog rides a giant golden coin like a surfboard into space, the wolf laughing.

scenes.say: Dogecoin was created in 2013 by two engineers, poking fun at crypto hype with a Shiba Inu meme.
In 2021, celebrity tweets and online hype sent it up by thousands of percent.
It has no max supply. Around five billion new coins are created every year.
It shows the power of community, and how fast hype can turn into a crash.
Follow for part 100: economic moats. Not financial advice.
Warren Buffett loves companies with a moat.
scenes.p: A medieval castle made of gold surrounded by a wide moat with crocodiles, the wolf standing on the castle wall like a king.

scenes.say: A moat is a lasting advantage that keeps competitors away, like the water around a castle.
It can be a powerful brand, like Coca-Cola.
Or a network effect: the more people use something, the more valuable it becomes for everyone.
Or high switching costs, or being the cheapest producer. Without a moat, profits get competed away.
Follow for part 101: Litecoin, the silver to Bitcoin's gold. Not financial advice.

101.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 101.

scenes.say: Litecoin was created in 2011 by Charlie Lee, as the silver to Bitcoin's gold.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a shiny silver coin next to a golden Bitcoin, comparing them in an elegant jewelry shop.

scenes.say: It's based on Bitcoin's code, but a new block comes every two and a half minutes instead of ten.
Its max supply is eighty-four million coins, four times Bitcoin's.
It's one of the oldest coins still around, often used for cheap and fast payments.
But being old doesn't guarantee growth. Many early coins slowly lost ground to newer ones.
Follow for part 102: Chainlink and oracle tokens. Not financial advice.

102.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 102.

scenes.say: Remember oracles? Chainlink is the biggest oracle network, and LINK is its token.
Independent node operators fetch real-world data, like prices, and deliver it to smart contracts.
They get paid in LINK for their work, and can be penalized for bad data.
Many big DeFi apps rely on Chainlink's price feeds.
But like any token, its price depends on demand, not just on how useful the network is.
Follow for part 103: Berkshire Hathaway. Not financial advice.
In 1965, Warren Buffett took control of a struggling textile company called Berkshire Hathaway.
scenes.p: An old brick textile mill with spinning machines and rolls of fabric, the wolf in a vintage suit walking in, 1960s style.

scenes.say: He used its cash to buy other businesses and stocks, and turned it into a giant.
Today it owns insurance companies like GEICO, a railroad, energy firms, and big stakes in companies like Apple.
It has never paid a dividend. Buffett preferred to reinvest the profits.
And one Class A share costs hundreds of thousands of dollars, because it has never been split.
Follow for part 104: privacy coins. Not financial advice.

104.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 104.

scenes.say: Bitcoin isn't private. Every transaction is public. Privacy coins try to change that.
scenes.p: The wolf in a dark hooded cloak walks through a foggy street at night holding a faintly glowing coin.

scenes.say: Monero, the best-known one, hides the sender, the receiver, and the amount.
Supporters say financial privacy is a basic right.
Regulators worry about crime, so several exchanges have delisted privacy coins.
If you buy them, know they can be harder to trade, and the rules differ by country.
Follow for part 105: the doji candle. Not financial advice.

105.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 105.

scenes.say: This tiny candle means buyers and sellers are tied. It's called a doji.
scenes.p: A giant thin candlestick shaped like a plus sign stands on a stage, the wolf studying it with a magnifying glass.

scenes.say: The open and the close are almost the same, so the body is just a thin line.
It shows indecision. Neither side won that period.
After a long rise or fall, a doji can hint that the trend is getting tired.
But alone it's just a clue. Wait for the next candle to confirm a direction.
Follow for part 106: Warren Buffett's rules. Not financial advice.
Warren Buffett's most famous rules fit into one minute.
Rule number one: never lose money. Rule number two: never forget rule number one.
Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful.
Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.
And his favorite holding period? Forever.
Follow for part 107: the hammer candle. Not financial advice.

107.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 107.

scenes.say: One single candle can warn you before a bounce. It's called the hammer.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a giant golden hammer shaped like a candlestick with a long handle, standing on top of a red falling chart.

scenes.say: It has a small body near the top, and a long wick below, at least twice the size of the body.
It means sellers pushed the price down hard, but buyers pushed it right back up.
It matters most after a downtrend, near a support level.
Wait for the next candle to confirm, and always place your stop below the wick.
Follow for part 108: the shooting star candle. Not financial advice.

108.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 108.

scenes.say: The shooting star looks pretty, but it often warns of a drop.
scenes.p: A glowing shooting star with a long tail crosses the night sky above a green rising chart that starts turning red, the wolf watching.

scenes.say: It's the opposite of the hammer: a small body at the bottom, and a long wick on top.
Buyers pushed the price up, but sellers slammed it back down before the close.
After a strong rally, near resistance, it can signal that buyers are running out of steam.
Confirmation matters. One candle is never the whole story.
Follow for part 109: Peter Lynch: invest in what you know. Not financial advice.
Peter Lynch ran Fidelity's Magellan fund from 1977 to 1990, and averaged about twenty-nine percent a year.
scenes.p: A cheerful white-haired investor at a desk piled high with company reports shakes hands with the wolf, 1980s office.

scenes.say: His famous advice: invest in what you know.
If you love a product and see everyone using it, that can be the start of an idea.
But only the start. He always studied the company's numbers before buying.
Know the business, know why you own it, and be ready to hold for years.
Follow for part 110: engulfing candles. Not financial advice.

110.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 110.

scenes.say: Watch this green candle completely swallow the red one before it.
scenes.p: A giant green candlestick character opens a huge mouth and swallows a smaller red candlestick, comic style, the wolf watching amazed.

scenes.say: That's a bullish engulfing: after a drop, one green body covers the entire previous red body.
It shows buyers suddenly taking control.
The mirror version, a red candle swallowing a green one, is a bearish engulfing. It can warn of a drop.
It's stronger near support or resistance, and with high volume. Never use it on its own.
Follow for part 111: the double top. Not financial advice.

111.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 111.

scenes.say: This chart shape has trapped buyers for decades. It's called the double top.
scenes.p: Two tall mountain peaks of exactly the same height, the wolf standing on a rope bridge between them, dramatic sky.

scenes.say: Price hits a high, pulls back, then fails to break that same high a second time.
It means buyers tried twice, and couldn't push any higher.
The signal comes when price breaks below the low between the two peaks, called the neckline.
Wait for that break. And remember, patterns fail often. Use a stop.
Follow for part 112: Benjamin Graham and Mr. Market. Not financial advice.
Benjamin Graham, Warren Buffett's teacher, invented a character called Mr. Market.
scenes.p: A moody cartoon businessman with wild hair knocks at the wolf's front door in the morning, offering papers with different prices, very emotional face.

scenes.say: Imagine a business partner who offers to buy or sell you shares every day, at a different price.
Some days he's euphoric and asks crazy prices. Other days he's depressed and sells cheap.
You don't have to trade with him. You can wait until his mood gives you a good deal.
The market is there to serve you, not to guide you.
Follow for part 113: the double bottom. Not financial advice.

113.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 113.

scenes.say: The double bottom is the double top turned upside down, and it can signal a recovery.
scenes.p: Two deep valleys of the same depth in a landscape, the wolf climbing out of the second valley toward bright sunlight.

scenes.say: Price falls to a low, bounces, falls back to the same low, and holds.
Sellers tried twice to push it lower, and failed.
The confirmation is a break above the high between the two lows.
Many traders place a stop just below the second low. Small risk, clear plan.
Follow for part 114: head and shoulders. Not financial advice.

114.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 114.

scenes.say: When you see this shape, be careful. It's called head and shoulders.
scenes.p: A mountain range with three peaks where the middle peak is the tallest, like a head between two shoulders, the wolf looking worried from below.

scenes.say: Three peaks: a left shoulder, a higher head, and a lower right shoulder.
The line connecting the lows between them is called the neckline.
When price breaks below that neckline, the uptrend may be over.
Some traders measure the head to estimate a target. But it fails often, so use a stop.
Follow for part 115: active versus passive investing. Not financial advice.
Should you try to beat the market, or simply own the market?
Active investing means picking stocks or timing trades to do better than an index.
Passive investing means buying the whole index and holding it, with low fees.
Over long periods, most active funds have failed to beat their index after fees.
Many people do both: a passive core, and a small active part to learn.
Follow for part 116: inverse head and shoulders. Not financial advice.

116.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 116.

scenes.say: Flip head and shoulders upside down, and you get one of the classic bottom patterns.
Three lows: a left shoulder, a deeper head, and a higher right shoulder.
When price breaks above the neckline, it can signal a new uptrend.
Rising volume on the breakout makes it more convincing.
As always: confirmation first, and a stop in case it fails.
Follow for part 117: the ascending triangle. Not financial advice.

117.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 117.

scenes.say: This shape often comes before a breakout to the upside. It's the ascending triangle.
scenes.p: The wolf climbs a staircase of rising steps squeezed under a flat glass ceiling, pressing his paws against the ceiling.

scenes.say: The top is flat: sellers keep defending the same price.
But the lows keep getting higher: buyers are stepping in earlier each time.
Pressure builds, and many traders wait for a close above the flat top.
Fakeouts happen. A stop below the last higher low keeps losses small.
Follow for part 118: fund fees that eat your returns. Not financial advice.
A fee of two percent a year sounds small. Over decades, it can eat a huge part of your money.
Fees are taken every single year, whether the fund does well or not.
Over thirty years, two percent versus a few tenths of a percent can cost you more than a third of your final money.
So look at the expense ratio before you buy any fund or ETF.
You can't control the market. You can control your costs.
Follow for part 119: the descending triangle. Not financial advice.

119.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 119.

scenes.say: The descending triangle is the bearish cousin of the ascending one.
The bottom is flat: buyers defend the same price again and again.
But the highs keep getting lower: sellers are getting more aggressive.
scenes.p: The wolf walks down a staircase of falling steps toward a flat glowing floor that is starting to crack.

scenes.say: When that flat support finally breaks, the drop can be fast.
Patterns are probabilities, not promises. Plan your exit before you enter.
Follow for part 120: the biggest lessons so far. Not financial advice.

120.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 120.

scenes.say: We're at part 120. Time to look back at the biggest lessons so far.
scenes.p: The wolf sits by a cozy fireplace reading a big leather book of memories, photos of past adventures on the wall, warm light.

scenes.say: Only invest what you can afford to lose, and never with borrowed money.
Secure your keys, never share your seed phrase, and use two-factor authentication.
Avoid leverage, use stop losses when you trade, and always have an exit plan.
Spread your risk, keep your fees low, and think in years, not days.
Follow for part 121: choosing a broker. Not financial advice.
To buy stocks or ETFs, you need a broker. Picking the right one matters.
scenes.p: The wolf walks down a futuristic shopping street where each shop window shows a different glowing trading app, comparing them.

scenes.say: First, make sure it's regulated in your country, and that your account is protected.
Compare the fees: trading commissions, currency exchange costs, and account fees.
Check which markets and products it offers, like ETFs or international stocks.
And a clear app with good support beats flashy features.
Follow for part 122: the bull flag. Not financial advice.

122.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 122.

scenes.say: This calm little pause often comes right before the next move up.
scenes.p: A tall flagpole shaped like a strong green upward line with a small flag waving on top, the wolf saluting next to it.

scenes.say: First, a strong push up. That's the pole.
Then the price drifts slightly down or sideways in a tight channel. That's the flag.
The signal is the breakout above the flag, ideally with rising volume.
Put your stop below the flag. If it fails, the loss stays small.
Follow for part 123: the bear flag. Not financial advice.

123.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 123.

scenes.say: The bear flag is the bull flag, turned upside down.
scenes.p: A big bear holds a red flag on a pole pointing downward from a cliff edge, the wolf watching cautiously.

scenes.say: A sharp drop first, then a weak bounce inside a tight channel.
Buyers try to recover, but they're not strong enough.
A break below the flag often continues the downtrend.
The lesson: a small bounce after a crash is not always a recovery.
Follow for part 124: fractional shares. Not financial advice.
Some stocks cost hundreds, even thousands of dollars per share. You don't need that much to start.
Many brokers let you buy fractional shares: just a slice of one share.
With ten dollars, you could own a tenth of a hundred-dollar share.
Your gains, losses and dividends are proportional to your slice.
Check the rules, though: some brokers don't let you transfer fractional shares elsewhere.
Follow for part 125: rising and falling wedges. Not financial advice.

125.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 125.

scenes.say: Wedges look like triangles, but they often break the opposite way.
scenes.p: Two glowing converging lines form a narrow wedge funnel tilted upward with a golden ball squeezed inside, the wolf watching.

scenes.say: A rising wedge climbs while getting narrower. Buyers are losing strength, and it often breaks down.
A falling wedge drops while narrowing. Sellers are tiring, and it often breaks up.
Volume usually shrinks inside the wedge, then expands on the breakout.
Wait for the break, then manage your risk.
Follow for part 126: the cup and handle. Not financial advice.

126.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 126.

scenes.say: This pattern looks like a teacup, and traders love it.
scenes.p: A giant golden teacup with a handle sits on a hill shaped like a smooth U, the wolf sipping tea from a tiny cup next to it.

scenes.say: First, a rounded bottom: the cup. Price slowly recovers to the old high.
Then a small dip: the handle. Nervous holders sell, and the price shakes out.
A breakout above the rim of the cup is the classic signal.
It can take weeks or months to form. Patience is part of the pattern.
Follow for part 127: options, and why they're risky. Not financial advice.
Options can turn a small amount into a fortune, or into zero, very fast.
scenes.p: The wolf sweats at a casino roulette table with stacks of chips, the wheel spinning, dramatic lights.

scenes.say: An option is a contract that gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price before a deadline.
A call option profits if the price goes up. A put profits if it goes down.
Time works against the buyer. Every day, the option loses some value, and many expire worthless.
Learn them slowly, with tiny amounts, or not at all.
Follow for part 128: breakouts and fakeouts. Not financial advice.

128.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 128.

scenes.say: The price breaks out, you buy, and it immediately falls back. That's a fakeout.
A breakout is when price moves through a key level, like resistance.
Fakeouts happen when there aren't enough buyers to keep it going.
Look for a candle that closes above the level, rising volume, or a retest that holds.
scenes.p: The wolf carefully taps a glowing floor with one foot to test it before stepping on it with his full weight.

scenes.say: And size your trade so that a fakeout is just a small, planned loss.
Follow for part 129: timeframes: which chart should you use. Not financial advice.

129.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 129.

scenes.say: The same coin can look bullish and bearish at the same time. It depends on the timeframe.
scenes.p: The wolf looks confused at three screens side by side: a jagged zoomed-in chart, a medium chart, and a huge smooth long-term chart.

scenes.say: Each candle can be one minute, one hour, one day, or one week.
Short timeframes are noisy. Long ones show the bigger trend.
Day traders watch minutes. Long-term investors look at daily and weekly charts.
Pick the timeframe that matches how long you plan to hold.
Follow for part 130: buying stocks on margin. Not financial advice.
Buying stocks on margin means buying with money borrowed from your broker.
It multiplies your gains, and your losses.
If your account drops too far, you get a margin call: add money, or be forced to sell.
scenes.p: The wolf's phone rings with an alarming red flashing screen while he holds his head, papers flying, at night.

scenes.say: And forced selling usually happens at the worst possible moment.
Plus, you pay interest on the loan for every day you hold.
Follow for part 131: multi-timeframe analysis. Not financial advice.

131.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 131.

scenes.say: Professional traders rarely look at just one chart.
Start with a big timeframe, like the weekly, to find the main trend.
Then zoom into the daily chart to find the key levels.
Then use a smaller timeframe to time your entry.
Trade in the direction of the bigger trend, and you're climbing with the market, not against it.
Follow for part 132: the MACD indicator. Not financial advice.

132.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 132.

scenes.say: The MACD is one of the most popular indicators in trading.
scenes.p: Two glowing curved lines crossing above a histogram of green and red bars on a giant screen, the wolf pointing at the crossing.

scenes.say: It compares a fast moving average with a slow one, usually twelve and twenty-six periods.
When the MACD line crosses above its signal line, momentum is turning up.
When it crosses below, momentum is turning down.
It lags behind price and gives false signals in sideways markets. Combine it with other tools.
Follow for part 133: the GameStop short squeeze. Not financial advice.
In January 2021, an internet crowd took on Wall Street, and a video game store went to the moon.
scenes.p: A huge crowd of cheering people holding phones launches a giant video game store shopping cart like a rocket over grand financial buildings, the wolf amazed.

scenes.say: Hedge funds had bet heavily against GameStop. More shares had been sold short than were available to trade.
Traders on Reddit started buying, forcing short sellers to buy back at higher and higher prices.
The stock went from under twenty dollars to over four hundred in a few weeks.
Then it crashed. Some got rich, many bought the top. A short squeeze is a wild ride, not a strategy.
Follow for part 134: Bollinger Bands. Not financial advice.

134.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 134.

scenes.say: Bollinger Bands wrap the price in a channel that breathes with volatility.
scenes.p: A glowing price line flows through a stretchy elastic tube that widens and narrows, the wolf stretching the tube with his paws.

scenes.say: The middle line is a twenty-period average. The outer bands sit two standard deviations above and below.
When the bands squeeze tight, volatility is low, and a big move often follows.
Touching the upper band doesn't automatically mean sell. In strong trends, price can ride the band.
Use the bands to read volatility, not as a magic buy or sell button.
Follow for part 135: EMA versus SMA. Not financial advice.

135.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 135.

scenes.say: Two moving averages, one big difference: speed.
A simple moving average gives every day the same weight.
An exponential moving average gives more weight to recent prices, so it reacts faster.
scenes.p: A sleek fast race car and a slow heavy truck drive side by side on a glowing road shaped like a chart, the wolf waving a racing flag.

scenes.say: Faster means earlier signals, but also more false ones.
Many traders use EMAs for short-term moves, and SMAs, like the two-hundred-day, for the big picture.
Follow for part 136: meme stocks. Not financial advice.
Some stocks move on memes, not on business results. They're called meme stocks.
Online communities pile in, prices explode, and social media fuels the fire.
GameStop and AMC were the famous examples in 2021.
Prices can disconnect completely from the company's real value, in both directions.
If you join the party, know that the music can stop at any second.
Follow for part 137: Fibonacci retracements. Not financial advice.

137.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 137.

scenes.say: Traders draw these lines on almost every chart. They come from a math sequence that's eight hundred years old.
scenes.p: The wolf draws glowing horizontal lines across a big chart, a golden spiral shell floating beside him and an ancient scroll on the desk.

scenes.say: Fibonacci retracements mark where a pullback might pause, often around thirty-eight, fifty, or sixty-two percent.
After a big move up, traders watch those levels for a bounce.
They work partly because so many people watch them.
Treat them as zones of interest, never as guarantees.
Follow for part 138: divergences. Not financial advice.

138.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 138.

scenes.say: Sometimes price says one thing, and momentum says another. That's a divergence.
scenes.p: Two paths split on a mountain, one climbing up and the other sloping down, the wolf standing at the fork with a compass.

scenes.say: Price makes a higher high, but the RSI makes a lower high. Momentum is fading.
That's a bearish divergence: an early warning of a possible reversal.
The opposite, lower lows in price with higher lows in the RSI, is a bullish divergence.
Divergences can last a long time before anything happens. Wait for price to confirm.
Follow for part 139: sector investing. Not financial advice.
The stock market is divided into sectors, like technology, healthcare, energy and banks.
scenes.p: A big city map divided into colorful districts: a tech district, a hospital district, an oil refinery district and a bank district, the wolf looking from above.

scenes.say: Different sectors shine at different times in the economic cycle.
Tech often leads in booms. Utilities and consumer staples tend to hold up better in slowdowns.
Sector ETFs let you invest in a whole industry at once.
But betting heavily on one sector means less diversification. Know where you're concentrated.
Follow for part 140: the risk to reward ratio. Not financial advice.

140.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 140.

scenes.say: You can lose most of your trades and still make money. Here's how.
Before you enter, decide where you're wrong, your stop, and where you take profit, your target.
If you risk one to make three, one win pays for three losses.
scenes.p: A balance scale where one small red weight is outweighed by three shiny gold coins on the other side, the wolf smiling.

scenes.say: Most beginners do the opposite: tiny wins, and huge losses.
Aim for trades where the reward is at least twice the risk.
Follow for part 141: the trading journal. Not financial advice.

141.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 141.

scenes.say: The best traders keep a diary. It's called a trading journal.
scenes.p: The wolf writes in a thick leather journal at night by a desk lamp, charts glowing on a screen behind him.

scenes.say: For every trade: why you entered, where your stop was, and how you felt.
After a month, patterns appear. Maybe you lose most trades on Fridays, or right after a big win.
The journal shows your mistakes before the market makes you pay for them twice.
What gets measured gets improved.
Follow for part 142: emerging markets. Not financial advice.
Some of the world's fastest-growing economies are called emerging markets.
scenes.p: The wolf flies in a hot air balloon over a rapidly growing city with cranes and new skyscrapers rising, sunrise.

scenes.say: Countries like India, Brazil and Indonesia, with growing populations and middle classes.
Growth can be fast, but so can trouble: politics, currency swings, and weaker investor protection.
Emerging market ETFs spread your money across many countries at once.
Many investors keep them as a smaller slice of a global portfolio.
Follow for part 143: backtesting. Not financial advice.

143.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 143.

scenes.say: Before you trust a strategy with real money, test it on the past.
scenes.p: The wolf in a retro-futuristic time machine cockpit watches old charts fly past on screens.

scenes.say: Backtesting means applying your rules to historical data, to see how they would have performed.
Clear rules only: entry, exit, stop, size. No decisions made with hindsight.
Beware of overfitting: a strategy tuned perfectly to the past often fails in the future.
A good backtest is a starting point, not a promise.
Follow for part 144: paper trading. Not financial advice.

144.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 144.

scenes.say: What if you could practice trading without risking a cent?
scenes.p: The wolf trades on a big screen made of paper, surrounded by paper money and paper coins, playful.

scenes.say: Paper trading means trading with fake money on real prices.
It's great for learning how orders work, and for testing a plan.
But fake money doesn't feel like real money. Fear and greed only show up when it's real.
Practice on paper, then start for real with tiny amounts.
Follow for part 145: currency risk. Not financial advice.
Your investment can go up, and you can still lose money. Blame the currency.
scenes.p: The wolf at an airport currency exchange counter looks shocked at a big board of glowing changing currency symbols.

scenes.say: If you live in Europe and buy US stocks, you're also betting on the dollar.
If the stock rises ten percent but the dollar falls ten percent against the euro, you're roughly flat.
Over long periods, currency moves often even out. In the short term, they can hurt.
Some ETFs are currency hedged to reduce this effect, usually with slightly higher fees.
Follow for part 146: overtrading. Not financial advice.

146.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 146.

scenes.say: More trades doesn't mean more profit. Usually, it means more losses.
scenes.p: The wolf frantically clicks on five keyboards and phones at once, surrounded by flying receipts, exhausted.

scenes.say: Every trade costs fees and spreads, and every extra trade is another chance to make a mistake.
Overtrading often comes from boredom, or from wanting to win back a loss.
The best setups are rare. Most of the time, the right move is to do nothing.
Set a maximum number of trades per day or per week, and stick to it.
Follow for part 147: revenge trading. Not financial advice.

147.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 147.

scenes.say: You lose a trade, you get angry, and you jump right back in, bigger. That's revenge trading.
scenes.p: The furious wolf, steam coming out of his ears, slams a huge stack of coins onto a trading desk, red screens all around.

scenes.say: It's emotion, not strategy. And it usually turns one loss into several.
The market doesn't know you lost. It doesn't owe you anything.
After a loss, step away. Take a walk, close the app, come back tomorrow.
scenes.p: The wolf takes a calm walk in a sunny green park, phone in his pocket, breathing fresh air, relaxed.

scenes.say: Some traders follow a simple rule: after two losses in a day, they stop.
Follow for part 148: bonds, explained. Not financial advice.
Bonds are the quiet side of investing. Here's how they work.
scenes.p: The wolf reads a fancy certificate with a ribbon and a wax seal in a calm, elegant old bank office, peaceful.

scenes.say: When you buy a bond, you're lending money to a government or a company.
In return, they pay you interest, called the coupon, and give your money back at the end.
Bonds are usually less volatile than stocks, but their returns are usually lower too.
The main risks: the borrower can't pay, or inflation eats your returns.
Follow for part 149: going long versus going short. Not financial advice.

149.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 149.

scenes.say: In trading, you can make money when prices fall too. It depends whether you're long or short.
Going long means you buy, hoping the price rises. That's what most investors do.
Going short means you profit if the price falls.
Long, your maximum loss is what you put in. Short, your losses can keep growing as long as the price rises.
That's why beginners should master going long before even thinking about shorts.
Follow for part 150: short selling, explained. Not financial advice.

150.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 150.

scenes.say: How do you sell something you don't own? That's short selling.
scenes.p: The wolf borrows a golden coin from a friendly banker at a counter, then sells it at a market stall, with a scheming grin.

scenes.say: You borrow an asset, sell it now, and hope to buy it back cheaper later.
If the price falls, you buy it back cheaper, return it, and keep the difference.
If it rises, you must buy back higher. And you pay to borrow, every day you wait.
Short squeezes, like GameStop, show how painful a short can get.
Follow for part 151: government bonds. Not financial advice.
When a country needs money, it borrows from investors by selling government bonds.
scenes.p: A grand government capitol building with columns, the wolf standing on the steps holding a ribbon-sealed certificate.

scenes.say: In the US they're called Treasuries. Germany has Bunds. Italy has BTPs.
Stable governments are seen as very safe borrowers, so they pay lower interest.
Riskier countries must pay higher interest to attract lenders.
And even safe bonds can lose value when interest rates rise. More on that soon.
Follow for part 152: futures versus spot. Not financial advice.

152.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 152.

scenes.say: Spot or futures? Two very different ways to trade crypto.
Spot means you buy the actual coin. You own it, and you can withdraw it.
Futures are contracts that bet on the price, often with leverage, without owning the coin.
They let you go long or short, but leverage can wipe you out fast.
For most beginners, spot is the safer place to start.
Follow for part 153: funding rates. Not financial advice.

153.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 153.

scenes.say: On crypto perpetual futures, traders pay each other a fee every few hours. It's called the funding rate.
scenes.p: Two groups of traders on opposite ends of a giant seesaw pass gold coins across to each other, the wolf in the middle as referee with a stopwatch.

scenes.say: When most traders are long, longs pay shorts. When most are short, shorts pay longs.
It keeps the futures price close to the spot price.
Very high funding means the crowd is extremely bullish, and crowded trades can unwind violently.
Watch it as a sentiment gauge, and remember it's a cost if you hold leveraged positions.
Follow for part 154: why bond prices fall when rates rise. Not financial advice.
Why do bond prices fall when interest rates rise? Here's the simple version.
Imagine your bond pays three percent. Then new bonds start paying five percent.
Nobody wants your three percent bond at full price anymore, so its price drops.
When rates fall, the opposite happens: older bonds with higher interest become more valuable.
Longer bonds react more. That's why bonds aren't risk-free, as 2022 painfully showed.
Follow for part 155: liquidation cascades. Not financial advice.

155.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 155.

scenes.say: Why does crypto sometimes drop ten percent in minutes? Often, it's a liquidation cascade.
scenes.p: A long row of giant dominoes made of gold coins falling one after another, the wolf running away from the falling line.

scenes.say: Many traders use leverage. When the price drops, some get liquidated, and their positions are sold automatically.
That selling pushes the price lower, which liquidates more traders, which pushes it even lower.
Then the forced selling dries up, and the price often bounces sharply.
Without leverage, you can't be liquidated. You can simply wait it out.
Follow for part 156: whales and market makers. Not financial advice.

156.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 156.

scenes.say: Behind every chart, there are big players moving big money.
Whales hold huge amounts of a coin. When they buy or sell, prices can move.
Market makers constantly place buy and sell orders, providing liquidity and earning the spread.
scenes.p: A busy market stall owner with many arms holding buy and sell price tags at the same time, coins flowing in both directions, the wolf watching.

scenes.say: On small coins, a few big wallets can dominate everything.
You can't control them. You can avoid illiquid coins, and manage your own risk.
Follow for part 157: real estate and REITs. Not financial advice.
Want to invest in real estate without buying a house? Meet REITs.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a tiny glowing model of an apartment building in his paw like a toy, a big city full of buildings behind him.

scenes.say: A REIT is a company that owns properties, like offices, warehouses or apartments, and rents them out.
In the US, REITs must pay out at least ninety percent of their taxable income, mostly as dividends.
You can buy them on the stock exchange, with small amounts, and sell anytime.
But they're sensitive to interest rates. When rates rise, REITs often fall.
Follow for part 158: stop hunts. Not financial advice.

158.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 158.

scenes.say: Your stop loss gets hit by a few cents, then the price flies back up. Was it hunted?
scenes.p: A hunter in a dark forest aims at a trail of small glowing red flags on the ground, the wolf hiding behind a tree.

scenes.say: Many traders put their stops in the same obvious places: just below support, or at round numbers.
A quick move through those levels triggers lots of stops at once, and big players use that liquidity.
Then the price often snaps right back.
Avoid the most obvious spots, give your stop some room, and size your trade so that room is affordable.
Follow for part 159: patience, the most underrated skill. Not financial advice.

159.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 159.

scenes.say: The most underrated skill in investing isn't intelligence. It's patience.
scenes.p: The wolf sits patiently on a park bench while the seasons change around him: falling leaves, snow, then spring flowers.

scenes.say: Most big gains come from a few big moves, and you only catch them if you're still holding.
Impatient investors jump from coin to coin, paying fees and buying tops.
Patience also means waiting for good prices, instead of chasing.
Time in the market, with a solid plan, does a lot of the heavy lifting.
Follow for part 160: savings accounts versus inflation. Not financial advice.
Your savings account says you have more money every year. In reality, you might have less.
scenes.p: The wolf happily reads his savings book while a sneaky little inflation monster quietly eats coins from his piggy bank.

scenes.say: If your account pays one percent and prices rise three percent, you lose about two percent of buying power a year.
Over ten years, that's a big loss, even though the number on your screen went up.
Cash is still important, for emergencies and short-term needs.
But for long-term money, many people look at investments that can beat inflation over time.
Follow for part 161: greed. Not financial advice.

161.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 161.

scenes.say: Greed doesn't feel like greed. It feels like confidence.
scenes.p: The wolf with glowing golden eyes reaches for a huge pile of coins balanced on the edge of a cliff.

scenes.say: You're up big, and instead of taking some profit, you buy more, at higher prices.
You ignore your plan, because this time feels different.
Greed peaks near the top, exactly when the risk is highest.
The fix: take partial profits at your targets, no matter how good it feels.
Follow for part 162: fear. Not financial advice.

162.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 162.

scenes.say: Fear makes you sell at the worst possible moment.
scenes.p: The wolf trembles under a blanket while a huge monster shadow looms on the wall, cast by a tiny toy chart.

scenes.say: Prices drop, headlines scream, and selling feels like the only way to stop the pain.
But the biggest fear often comes near the bottom, right before things recover.
Fear helps when it stops crazy risks. It hurts when it makes you abandon a good plan.
So prepare before the crash: only invest what you can hold through a big drop.
Follow for part 163: inflation, explained. Not financial advice.
Why does everything get more expensive every year? That's inflation.
scenes.p: The wolf at a supermarket checkout is shocked by a very long receipt, his shopping cart only half full.

scenes.say: Inflation means prices rise over time, so each unit of money buys a little less.
It can come from too much money chasing too few goods, or from rising costs like energy.
Many central banks aim for about two percent a year.
When it runs much higher, savings lose value fast, and interest rates usually rise to fight it.
Follow for part 164: loss aversion. Not financial advice.

164.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 164.

scenes.say: Losing a hundred dollars hurts more than winning a hundred dollars feels good. It's called loss aversion.
scenes.p: A balance scale where a small red weight outweighs a big pile of green gains, the wolf surprised.

scenes.say: Research suggests losses feel roughly twice as strong as gains of the same size.
So we hold losing trades too long, hoping to break even.
And we sell winners too early, just to lock in the good feeling.
A written plan with stops and targets protects you from your own brain.
Follow for part 165: confirmation bias. Not financial advice.

165.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 165.

scenes.say: Once you own a coin, your brain starts looking only for good news about it.
scenes.p: The wolf wears giant rose-colored glasses that make every chart look green, while the real charts behind him are red.

scenes.say: That's confirmation bias: we look for information that agrees with us, and ignore the rest.
Social media makes it worse. We follow people who already agree with us.
Before you buy, write down what would prove you wrong.
And read the best arguments against your investment, not just the ones for it.
Follow for part 166: compound interest. Not financial advice.
It's often called the eighth wonder of the world: compound interest.
scenes.p: A small golden snowball rolls down a long snowy mountain and becomes a gigantic golden snowball at the bottom, the wolf amazed.

scenes.say: Compounding means you earn returns on your returns, not just on what you put in.
A thousand dollars growing at seven percent a year becomes about seven thousand six hundred dollars in thirty years.
The first years look boring. The magic happens at the end.
That's why starting early matters more than starting big.
Follow for part 167: the sunk cost trap. Not financial advice.

167.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 167.

scenes.say: I've already lost so much, I can't sell now. That thought has cost people fortunes.
scenes.p: The wolf keeps pouring gold coins into a sinking boat that is already half underwater.

scenes.say: It's the sunk cost trap: money already lost shapes your next decision.
But the market doesn't care what you paid. Only the future matters.
Ask yourself: if I had the cash today, would I buy this, at this price?
If the answer is no, holding is just hoping.
Follow for part 168: anchoring to old prices. Not financial advice.

168.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 168.

scenes.say: It was worth twice as much last year, so it must be cheap now. Not so fast.
scenes.p: The wolf sits in a small boat tied to a heavy rusty anchor with an old price tag hanging on it, unable to move.

scenes.say: Anchoring means getting stuck on an old price, like the all-time high, or what you paid.
Many coins that fell ninety percent never returned to their old highs.
A price is only cheap compared to future value, not compared to the past.
Judge every investment on what it's worth today, and where it's going.
Follow for part 169: the rule of 72. Not financial advice.
Want to know how fast your money doubles? Use the rule of 72.
scenes.p: The wolf at a chalkboard draws one pile of coins turning into two piles, a glowing clock above the board.

scenes.say: Divide seventy-two by your yearly return. The answer is roughly how many years it takes to double.
At eight percent a year, money doubles in about nine years.
It works for inflation too: at four percent inflation, prices double in about eighteen years.
And for debt: at twenty-four percent interest, what you owe doubles in about three years.
Follow for part 170: herd mentality. Not financial advice.

170.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 170.

scenes.say: When everyone is buying the same coin, it feels safe. It usually isn't.
scenes.p: A huge herd of sheep runs toward a cliff edge following a glowing coin, the wolf standing still and watching.

scenes.say: Herd mentality means following the crowd instead of your own analysis.
Crowds tend to buy after big rises, and sell after big drops.
By the time your friends and family talk about a coin, the easy gains are often gone.
Have your own plan, and be okay doing something different from the crowd.
Follow for part 171: overconfidence after a win. Not financial advice.

171.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 171.

scenes.say: The most dangerous moment in trading? Right after a big win.
scenes.p: The wolf wears a crown and a cape on a throne made of coins, overconfident, while the throne cracks beneath him.

scenes.say: Wins make us feel smart, so we take bigger risks.
One lucky trade can lead to bigger positions, more leverage, and skipped stop losses.
And the market often takes back the gains, plus more.
After a big win, keep the same size and the same rules. Consistency beats excitement.
Follow for part 172: an emergency fund comes first. Not financial advice.
Before you invest a single dollar, build this first: an emergency fund.
scenes.p: The wolf puts cash into a big glass jar with a red cross symbol on a kitchen shelf, responsible.

scenes.say: It's cash set aside for surprises: a lost job, a medical bill, a broken car.
Many experts suggest three to six months of expenses.
Without it, one bad month can force you to sell investments at the worst time.
Keep it safe and easy to reach, not in volatile assets like crypto.
Follow for part 173: checking prices too often. Not financial advice.

173.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 173.

scenes.say: If you check prices every five minutes, you're not investing. You're stressing.
scenes.p: The wolf surrounded by ten phones all showing price charts, dark circles under his eyes, late at night.

scenes.say: Short-term moves are mostly noise.
Constant checking leads to emotional decisions: panic selling, and FOMO buying.
Set price alerts for the levels that matter, and close the app.
Long-term investors check weekly or monthly, and sleep a lot better.
Follow for part 174: social media noise. Not financial advice.

174.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 174.

scenes.say: Every day, social media tells you a new coin will change your life.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in a storm of floating smartphones shouting through megaphones with flashing rockets, covering his ears.

scenes.say: Most posts are opinions, hype, or paid promotions, not research.
Algorithms show you what keeps you scrolling, not what's true.
Use social media for ideas, then verify them on your own.
Mute the noise, follow fewer people, and stick to your plan.
Follow for part 175: paying off expensive debt first. Not financial advice.
Investing while carrying credit card debt is like filling a bucket with a hole in it.
scenes.p: The wolf pours water from a golden watering can into a bucket with a big hole at the bottom, water leaking out.

scenes.say: Credit cards often charge twenty percent interest or more.
Very few investments reliably earn that much.
Paying off expensive debt is like a guaranteed return equal to its interest rate.
Clear the expensive debt first, then invest what's left.
Follow for part 176: paid influencer promotions. Not financial advice.

176.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 176.

scenes.say: That influencer loves a new coin. Did you ask who's paying?
scenes.p: A smiling influencer films himself with a ring light while a shadowy hand slips him a bag of money behind the camera.

scenes.say: Many crypto promotions are paid, and not always clearly disclosed.
Some influencers get tokens cheap, promote them, then sell to their own followers.
In many countries, hidden paid promotions are illegal, but they still happen.
Treat every enthusiastic post as an ad, until proven otherwise.
Follow for part 177: setting realistic goals. Not financial advice.

177.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 177.

scenes.say: Turning a thousand into a million in a year is not a goal. It's a lottery ticket.
scenes.p: The wolf aims a tiny dart at an impossibly far target on a distant mountain, while a realistic target stands right in front of him.

scenes.say: Unrealistic goals push you into leverage, meme coins and big risks.
Realistic goals are boring: steady saving, reasonable returns, years of patience.
Set goals you control: how much you save, how much you learn, how well you follow your plan.
Small wins, repeated for years, become big results.
Follow for part 178: the 50/30/20 budget. Not financial advice.
Don't know where your money goes every month? Try the fifty, thirty, twenty rule.
scenes.p: The wolf divides a big golden pie of coins into three slices of different sizes on a kitchen table, focused.

scenes.say: Fifty percent of your income for needs: rent, food, bills, transport.
Thirty percent for wants: dinners, trips, hobbies.
Twenty percent for your future: savings, debt payoff, investments.
It's not a strict law, just a simple starting point. The key is that saving comes first, not last.
Follow for part 179: writing your investment plan. Not financial advice.

179.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 179.

scenes.say: Most people who lose money in crypto never wrote down a plan.
scenes.p: The wolf signs a neat one-page plan on an elegant desk with a fountain pen, a calm and confident face.

scenes.say: Your plan answers simple questions: how much you invest, in what, and for how long.
When you take profit, and when you admit you're wrong.
How much of your money can be in risky coins, and how much stays safe.
Write it on a calm day, and follow it on the crazy days.
Follow for part 180: why discipline beats talent. Not financial advice.

180.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 180.

scenes.say: In investing, discipline beats talent. Every time.
scenes.p: A tortoise wearing a tiny suit crosses a finish line ahead of a tired hare, the wolf cheering as the referee.

scenes.say: Smart people still lose money when they break their own rules.
Discipline means doing the boring things consistently: saving, sticking to stops, not chasing.
It's not exciting, and that's exactly why most people don't do it.
Small, disciplined steps repeated for years beat brilliant moves made once.
Follow for part 181: pay yourself first. Not financial advice.
Most people save what's left at the end of the month. Usually, nothing is left.
scenes.p: The wolf turns his empty wallet upside down at the end of the month, only a moth flying out.

scenes.say: Paying yourself first flips it: the moment you get paid, a fixed amount goes straight to savings.
Then you live on the rest.
Automate it with a standing transfer, so you don't even have to think about it.
Start small, even five percent, and raise it every time your income grows.
Follow for part 182: when to take a break. Not financial advice.

182.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 182.

scenes.say: Sometimes the best trade is no trade at all.
scenes.p: The wolf lies in a hammock on a quiet beach, his phone turned off on a little table next to him.

scenes.say: After a string of losses, your judgment gets worse, not better.
Stress makes you chase, overtrade and ignore your plan.
Taking a few days off resets your mind. The market will still be there.
Professional traders take breaks on purpose. You should too.
Follow for part 183: never invest borrowed money. Not financial advice.

183.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 183.

scenes.say: Never invest borrowed money in crypto. Here's why this rule exists.
scenes.p: The wolf walks a tightrope over a deep canyon carrying a heavy bag of borrowed money, wobbling.

scenes.say: Prices can fall fifty percent or more. Your debt doesn't fall with them.
You still owe the full amount, plus interest, even if your investment is wiped out.
Borrowed money also creates pressure, and pressure creates bad decisions.
Invest only money you own, and could afford to lose.
Follow for part 184: lifestyle inflation. Not financial advice.
You earn more than five years ago. So why do you still have nothing left?
scenes.p: The wolf's salary grows like a tall stack of coins, but his shopping bags, gadgets and car grow even faster around him.

scenes.say: It's called lifestyle inflation: spending rises every time income rises.
A bigger car, a nicer phone, more dinners out. Each one feels small.
Together, they eat every raise you get.
When your income goes up, save at least half of the raise. Your future self will thank you.
Follow for part 185: thinking in years, not days. Not financial advice.

185.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 185.

scenes.say: Crypto moves fast. Wealth is built slowly.
scenes.p: The wolf stands at the start of a very long road stretching to the horizon, a small backpack on his shoulders.

scenes.say: Daily price moves feel huge, but in five years, most of them won't matter.
Long-term investors judge their decisions in years, not days.
Thinking long term makes it easier to ignore the noise and stick to the plan.
Ask yourself: will this matter in five years? Most of the time, it won't.
Follow for part 186: strong passwords and password managers. Not financial advice.

186.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 186.

scenes.say: A weak password is an open door to your crypto.
scenes.p: A big front door made of gold coins left wide open with the key still in the lock, a sneaky thief tiptoeing toward it.

scenes.say: Use long, unique passwords for every account. Never reuse the same one.
A password manager creates and remembers them for you.
If one website gets hacked, the others stay safe.
And protect the password manager itself with a strong master password and two-factor authentication.
Follow for part 187: tracking your net worth. Not financial advice.
Want to know if you're really getting richer? Track your net worth.
scenes.p: The wolf adds up gold coins, a small house model and a stack of cash on a big scale, minus a pile of bills on the other side.

scenes.say: Net worth is everything you own, minus everything you owe.
Add up savings, investments and property. Subtract loans, cards and debts.
Update it every few months, and watch the trend, not the daily swings.
It's the simplest scoreboard for your financial life.
Follow for part 188: authenticator apps versus SMS codes. Not financial advice.

188.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 188.

scenes.say: Two-factor authentication is great. But SMS codes are its weakest form.
scenes.p: The wolf holds two phones: one showing a flimsy paper text message, the other showing a strong glowing authenticator shield.

scenes.say: Text messages can be intercepted, or stolen through your phone number.
Authenticator apps generate codes on your device, without going through your phone carrier.
Hardware security keys are even stronger for important accounts.
Switch your exchange and email to an authenticator app today. It takes five minutes.
Follow for part 189: SIM swap attacks. Not financial advice.

189.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 189.

scenes.say: Someone can steal your phone number without touching your phone. It's called a SIM swap.
scenes.p: A sneaky thief pulls a glowing SIM card out of the air with a magnet while the wolf looks at his phone losing signal.

scenes.say: The attacker convinces your phone company to move your number to their SIM card.
Then they receive your SMS codes, and reset your passwords.
Protect yourself: ask your carrier for a SIM lock or a port-out PIN.
And don't use SMS for two-factor authentication on accounts that hold money.
Follow for part 190: time in the market versus timing the market. Not financial advice.
Trying to time the market sounds smart. The numbers say otherwise.
scenes.p: The wolf tries to catch a lightning bolt with a butterfly net in a stormy sky, frustrated.

scenes.say: Many of the best days in the stock market come right after some of the worst.
Missing just a handful of the best days can cut your long-term returns roughly in half.
Staying invested through the ups and downs has historically beaten jumping in and out.
Time in the market beats timing the market.
Follow for part 191: securing your email. Not financial advice.

191.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 191.

scenes.say: Your email is the master key to all your accounts.
scenes.p: A giant golden envelope with a keyhole sits at the center of a ring of locked doors, the wolf holding the key.

scenes.say: If someone takes your email, they can reset the password of your exchange, your bank, everything.
Use a strong unique password and an authenticator app on your email.
Consider a separate email address used only for your financial accounts.
And check the security settings for unknown devices and forwarding rules.
Follow for part 192: fake browser extensions. Not financial advice.

192.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 192.

scenes.say: A browser extension can read everything you do online, including your wallet.
scenes.p: A tiny sneaky robot hides inside a puzzle piece plugged into a web browser, peeking at the wolf's crypto wallet.

scenes.say: Fake wallet extensions copy real names and logos to trick you.
Once installed, they can steal your seed phrase or swap transaction details.
Install wallet extensions only from the official website, and check the developer.
Remove extensions you don't use. Fewer extensions, fewer risks.
Follow for part 193: risk tolerance and time horizon. Not financial advice.
Two people can buy the same investment, and only one of them should.
scenes.p: Two wolves side by side: one young with a skateboard and a long road ahead, one older with a cane near the finish line.

scenes.say: Risk tolerance is how much loss you can handle, financially and emotionally, without panicking.
Time horizon is when you'll need the money.
Money for next year should be safe. Money for twenty years can take more risk.
Know both before you choose anything. The right investment depends on you.
Follow for part 194: token approvals, and how to revoke them. Not financial advice.

194.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 194.

scenes.say: You may have given an app permission to spend your tokens, forever.
scenes.p: The wolf signs a never-ending glowing scroll that keeps unrolling, while tiny hands quietly take coins from his wallet.

scenes.say: When you use a DeFi app, you often approve it to move your tokens.
Many approvals are unlimited, and stay active long after you stop using the app.
If that app gets hacked, your tokens can be drained.
Use a token approval checker for your wallet, and revoke the approvals you don't need.
Follow for part 195: address poisoning. Not financial advice.

195.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 195.

scenes.say: You copy an address from your history, send your crypto, and it's gone. Address poisoning.
scenes.p: Two almost identical glowing addresses on scrolls side by side, one with a tiny hidden skull, the wolf comparing them.

scenes.say: Scammers send tiny transactions from addresses that look like ones you've used.
The first and last characters match, so it looks right at a glance.
Never copy addresses from your transaction history.
Use your address book, check the whole address, and send a small test first.
Follow for part 196: asset allocation, explained. Not financial advice.
The biggest decision in investing isn't which stock or coin. It's how you split your money.
scenes.p: The wolf arranges glass jars of different sizes on a shelf: stocks, bonds, gold, cash and a small crypto jar.

scenes.say: That's asset allocation: how much goes into stocks, bonds, cash, gold, or crypto.
Different assets behave differently in good and bad times.
A mix you can stick with through a crash is better than a perfect one you abandon.
Review it once or twice a year, and rebalance when it drifts.
Follow for part 197: fake support on Telegram and Discord. Not financial advice.

197.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 197.

scenes.say: You post a question in a crypto group, and support messages you within seconds. It's a trap.
scenes.p: A friendly-looking support agent avatar on a phone screen with a fox tail hidden behind it, the wolf suspicious.

scenes.say: Real support teams almost never message you first in Telegram or Discord.
Fake agents send links to fix your wallet, or ask for your seed phrase.
Some even show fake staff badges and official-looking logos.
Only use support from the official website or app. Never through direct messages.
Follow for part 198: pig butchering scams. Not financial advice.

198.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 198.

scenes.say: A friendly stranger texts you by mistake. Weeks later, your savings are gone. It's called pig butchering.
scenes.p: A friendly smiling face on a phone screen that is actually a mask with a sinister shadow behind it, the wolf holding the phone, suspicious.

scenes.say: Scammers build a relationship over weeks, as a friend or even a romantic partner.
Then they show you their amazing profits, and invite you to a special trading platform.
You see gains on the screen, you deposit more, and then you can't withdraw. The platform is fake.
Never invest through someone you only know online. Ever.
Follow for part 199: why people buy gold. Not financial advice.
For thousands of years, people have trusted one metal more than any currency: gold.
scenes.p: An ancient temple treasury full of golden coins from different eras, the wolf holding a torch in awe.

scenes.say: It doesn't rust, it's rare, and no government can print it.
Central banks hold gold in their reserves, and many have been buying more in recent years.
In a crisis, investors often run to gold as a safe haven.
But gold pays no interest and no dividends. Its value depends on what others will pay for it.
Follow for part 200: Ponzi schemes. Not financial advice.

200.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 200.

scenes.say: Old investors get paid with new investors' money. It works, until it doesn't.
scenes.p: A tall tower of cartoon people standing on each other's shoulders, the bottom ones crumbling, the wolf stepping back.

scenes.say: It's called a Ponzi scheme, after Charles Ponzi, who ran one in the 1920s.
The biggest ever was Bernie Madoff's, which collapsed in 2008 with tens of billions in paper losses.
In crypto, they hide behind words like staking, mining pools or trading bots, with fixed high returns.
Steady high returns with no clear source? That's the classic warning sign.
Follow for part 201: pump and dump groups. Not financial advice.

201.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 201.

scenes.say: A group announces a coin, everyone buys at the same second, and the price explodes. Then it collapses.
scenes.p: A crowd of cartoon people pumps up a giant balloon shaped like a coin, while a few people at the top sneak away with bags of money.

scenes.say: The organizers buy first, quietly, at low prices.
Members pile in, and outsiders see the spike and jump in too.
The organizers sell into all that buying, and the price crashes within minutes.
Most members lose money, and these schemes are illegal in many countries. Stay away.
Follow for part 202: gold and inflation. Not financial advice.
Gold is called an inflation hedge. The truth is more complicated.
scenes.p: A big golden umbrella protects the wolf from a rain of shrinking paper banknotes.

scenes.say: During the high inflation of the 1970s, gold rose enormously.
But after its 1980 peak, gold took almost three decades to get back to that price.
Over very long periods, gold has roughly kept its buying power. Over shorter ones, it can disappoint.
Many investors see it as insurance, a small part of a portfolio, not a get-rich plan.
Follow for part 203: fake trading bots with guaranteed profits. Not financial advice.

203.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 203.

scenes.say: A bot that makes you ten percent a month, guaranteed? That's not a bot. It's a scam.
scenes.p: A shiny robot with a fake smile holds a big golden guarantee seal, while its open back shows it is completely empty inside.

scenes.say: Real trading strategies have losing months. Nobody can guarantee returns.
Scam bots ask you to send money to their wallet, or to a platform they control.
The dashboard shows growing profits, until you try to withdraw.
Legit tools never hold your funds and never promise fixed profits. If one does, walk away.
Follow for part 204: romance scams. Not financial advice.

204.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 204.

scenes.say: They say they love you. Then they ask for crypto.
scenes.p: A heart-shaped balloon with a fishing hook hanging from it floats toward the wolf at sunset.

scenes.say: Romance scammers use fake profiles and stolen photos on dating apps and social media.
They build trust for weeks. Then comes an emergency, or an investment opportunity.
They prefer crypto because it's fast, and hard to reverse.
If someone you've never met in person asks for money, stop, and talk to a friend first.
Follow for part 205: gold versus Bitcoin. Not financial advice.
Gold or Bitcoin: which one is the real store of value?
Gold has thousands of years of history, real-world uses, and central banks own it.
Bitcoin is digital, easy to send worldwide, and its supply is fixed at twenty-one million.
But Bitcoin is far more volatile. It can lose more than half its value in a year.
Many investors don't choose. They hold a bit of both, sized to their risk.
Follow for part 206: fake exchanges and fake apps. Not financial advice.

206.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 206.

scenes.say: The app looks professional, the logo looks real, and your money disappears.
scenes.p: A shiny app on a phone screen peels off like a sticker revealing a dark empty void underneath, the wolf shocked.

scenes.say: Scammers build fake exchanges, and fake copies of real wallet apps.
They promote them through ads, messages, and search results.
Check the exact web address, download only from official sources, and search for warnings.
And if withdrawing requires paying a fee or a tax first, it's a scam.
Follow for part 207: QR code scams. Not financial advice.

207.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 207.

scenes.say: Scanning a QR code can empty your wallet.
scenes.p: A QR code sticker on a parking meter with a tiny hidden skull in the corner, the wolf about to scan it with his phone.

scenes.say: Scammers put fake QR codes on posters, in emails, and even on parking meters.
The code can open a fake website, or a transaction that sends your crypto to them.
Some ask you to scan a code to receive money. Receiving crypto never requires you to sign anything.
Before you approve anything, read exactly what you're signing.
Follow for part 208: how to invest in gold. Not financial advice.
Want some gold in your portfolio? There are three main ways to do it.
scenes.p: Three doors in a golden hallway, one showing a gold bar, one a chart on a screen, one a mining helmet, the wolf choosing.

scenes.say: Physical gold: bars and coins. You own it directly, but you need safe storage.
Gold ETFs: funds that hold gold. Easy to buy and sell from a broker, with a small yearly fee.
Gold mining stocks: companies that dig it out. They often move more than gold, in both directions.
Whatever you choose, gold is usually a slice of a portfolio, not the whole thing.
Follow for part 209: recovery scams. Not financial advice.

209.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 209.

scenes.say: You got scammed. Then someone offers to recover your crypto, for a fee. That's the second scam.
scenes.p: A fake superhero in a cape offers help to the wolf while hiding an empty money bag behind his back.

scenes.say: Recovery scammers find victims in comments and groups, posing as hackers or lawyers.
They ask for an upfront fee, then more fees, and recover nothing.
Blockchain transactions usually can't be reversed by anyone you find online.
Report the scam to the police and the exchange involved. Never pay someone who promises recovery.
Follow for part 210: crypto inheritance planning. Not financial advice.

210.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 210.

scenes.say: If something happened to you tomorrow, could your family access your crypto?
scenes.p: The wolf as an old grandfather hands a small locked chest and a sealed letter to a young wolf, warm living room.

scenes.say: Without your keys or instructions, coins can be lost forever.
Write a clear guide: what you own, where it is, and how to access it.
Keep it secure, and never leave the seed phrase where strangers might find it.
Some people use a lawyer, a will, or a multisig setup. Plan it now, while it's easy.
Follow for part 211: silver, the double life metal. Not financial advice.
Silver lives a double life: precious metal, and industrial workhorse.
scenes.p: The wolf juggles a shiny silver coin and a small solar panel in a workshop that is half jewelry shop, half tech lab.

scenes.say: It's used in jewelry and coins, but also in electronics and solar panels.
So its price depends on investors, and on the economy.
Silver is usually more volatile than gold, with bigger swings both ways.
Some investors hold a little silver next to gold, knowing it's the bumpier ride.
Follow for part 212: multisig wallets. Not financial advice.

212.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 212.

scenes.say: What if stealing one key wasn't enough to steal your crypto?
scenes.p: A vault door with three separate locks, the wolf and two friends each holding a different key.

scenes.say: A multisig wallet needs several keys to approve a transaction. For example, two out of three.
Lose one key, and you can still reach your funds with the other two.
And a thief with one key can't move anything.
It's more complex to set up, but great for large amounts, companies and families.
Follow for part 213: keeping your holdings private. Not financial advice.

213.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 213.

scenes.say: The biggest security risk might be telling people how much crypto you own.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a finger to his lips in a shh gesture while hiding a small treasure chest behind his back.

scenes.say: Bragging online makes you a target for hackers, scammers, and even physical threats.
Don't post screenshots of your balance, or your wallet addresses.
Use different wallets for public payments and for long-term savings.
Quiet money is safer money.
Follow for part 214: the gold to silver ratio. Not financial advice.
How many ounces of silver does it take to buy one ounce of gold? That number is a famous indicator.
scenes.p: A balance scale with one gold bar on one side and a tall stack of silver bars on the other, the wolf counting them.

scenes.say: It's called the gold to silver ratio.
It changes a lot. In 2020, it briefly went above one hundred twenty.
When the ratio is very high, some investors think silver is cheap compared to gold. When it's low, the opposite.
It's a rough guide, not a signal. Metals can stay cheap or expensive for years.
Follow for part 215: backing up your seed phrase in two places. Not financial advice.

215.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 215.

scenes.say: One copy of your seed phrase is one fire away from disaster.
scenes.p: A small paper card burns on a desk while the wolf holds a steel plate backup safely in his other paw.

scenes.say: Keep at least two backups, in two different safe places.
Paper burns and fades. Metal backups survive fire and water.
Never store your seed phrase in the cloud, in an email, or in a photo.
And check once a year that your backups are still there, and readable.
Follow for part 216: buying a hardware wallet safely. Not financial advice.

216.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 216.

scenes.say: A hardware wallet protects your crypto, unless the device itself was tampered with.
scenes.p: The wolf inspects a small hardware wallet box with a magnifying glass, checking the seal, at a desk.

scenes.say: Buy only from the official manufacturer or authorized sellers. Never second-hand.
A real device never comes with a seed phrase already written for you.
Set it up yourself, and write down the seed phrase it generates.
And update the firmware only through the official app.
Follow for part 217: platinum and palladium. Not financial advice.
Platinum and palladium are rarer than gold, and most people never think of investing in them.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a shiny platinum bar next to a gold bar under bright lights, comparing their shine.

scenes.say: Both are used mainly in car catalytic converters, which clean exhaust gases.
Most of the supply comes from just a few places, especially South Africa and Russia.
That makes prices very sensitive to car sales, mining problems and politics.
And the shift to electric cars adds a big question mark. High potential, high risk.
Follow for part 218: verifying addresses on your hardware wallet. Not financial advice.

218.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 218.

scenes.say: Your hardware wallet has a tiny screen for one big reason.
scenes.p: The wolf compares the tiny screen of a hardware wallet with a laptop screen side by side, magnifying glass in paw.

scenes.say: Malware on your computer can swap the address you're sending to, without you noticing.
The wallet's own screen is something malware can't change.
Before you confirm, compare the full address on the device with the one you intended.
If they don't match, cancel. The device screen is the one to trust.
Follow for part 219: why Federal Reserve meetings move crypto. Not financial advice.

219.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 219.

scenes.say: Eight times a year, a meeting in Washington can move Bitcoin by thousands of dollars.
scenes.p: A grand round meeting table in a classical building with serious officials around it, a giant glowing Bitcoin hovering above, the wolf peeking through the door.

scenes.say: The Federal Reserve sets US interest rates, which affect money all over the world.
Higher rates make borrowing expensive and safe assets more attractive, which often hurts risky assets like crypto.
Lower rates, or hints of cuts, often support risk assets.
And markets react not just to the decision, but to the surprise versus expectations.
Follow for part 220: copper, the metal with a PhD in economics. Not financial advice.
Traders call it Doctor Copper, because it seems to have a PhD in economics.
scenes.p: A wise copper statue wearing a graduation cap and glasses stands in a factory, the wolf shaking its hand.

scenes.say: Copper is in houses, cars, power grids and electronics.
When the economy grows, demand for copper rises. When it slows, demand falls.
So copper prices are often watched as an early signal of economic health.
And electric cars and power grids need lots of it, which keeps copper in the spotlight.
Follow for part 221: crypto and the stock market. Not financial advice.

221.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 221.

scenes.say: Crypto was supposed to be separate from Wall Street. Lately, they often move together.
scenes.p: The wolf holds two puppets on strings, one shaped like a stock exchange building and one like a Bitcoin coin, dancing in sync.

scenes.say: Since big institutions entered crypto, Bitcoin has often moved with tech stocks.
When investors fear risk, they sell both. When they feel confident, they buy both.
The link isn't constant. Sometimes crypto goes its own way.
If you own both, know that they may fall together in a crisis.
Follow for part 222: liquidity cycles. Not financial advice.

222.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 222.

scenes.say: Sometimes everything goes up together. Often, it's not about the assets. It's about liquidity.
scenes.p: A big golden tide rises in a harbor and lifts all the boats together, the wolf standing on the pier.

scenes.say: Liquidity is how much money is flowing through the financial system.
When central banks cut rates and add money, it often flows into stocks, crypto and real estate.
When they tighten, money dries up, and risky assets usually suffer first.
Watching liquidity helps explain moves that the news alone can't.
Follow for part 223: lithium and the battery boom. Not financial advice.
The metal inside your phone and electric cars had one of the wildest price rides of the decade.
scenes.p: The wolf rides a giant glowing battery like a rocket that then dives down like a roller coaster.

scenes.say: Lithium is a key ingredient in rechargeable batteries.
As electric car sales soared, lithium prices exploded in 2021 and 2022.
Then new supply arrived, demand cooled, and prices crashed by around eighty percent.
