Boom and bust is normal in commodities. A big trend doesn't mean prices only go up.
Follow for part 224: institutional adoption. Not financial advice.

224.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 224.

scenes.say: Crypto used to be for hobbyists. Now some of the world's biggest investment firms are in.
scenes.p: Serious bankers in suits walk into a futuristic crypto building carrying briefcases, the wolf holding the door open.

scenes.say: Asset managers launched Bitcoin ETFs, and some companies hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets.
Banks are building custody and trading services for their clients.
Institutions bring money and legitimacy, but also stronger links to traditional markets.
It doesn't make crypto safe. It makes it bigger, and more connected.
Follow for part 225: crypto rules in Europe: MiCA. Not financial advice.

225.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 225.

scenes.say: Europe now has one rulebook for crypto. It's called MiCA.
scenes.p: The wolf reads a big official rulebook with a circle of golden stars on its cover in front of a modern parliament building.

scenes.say: MiCA stands for Markets in Crypto-Assets, and it applies across the European Union.
Crypto service providers need a license, and must follow rules on security, disclosure and customer protection.
Stablecoin issuers face strict rules on their reserves.
For users, it means more protection, and fewer shady platforms targeting Europe.
Follow for part 226: rare earth metals. Not financial advice.
Your phone, electric cars and wind turbines all depend on metals most people have never heard of.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a handful of glittering colorful minerals in a mine, a smartphone and a tiny wind turbine floating above them.

scenes.say: They're called rare earth elements, used in powerful magnets and electronics.
They're not actually that rare, but they're hard and dirty to process.
China handles most of the world's processing, which makes them a political issue.
Prices can jump on trade tensions. Exciting story, volatile investment.
Follow for part 227: stablecoin regulation. Not financial advice.

227.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 227.

scenes.say: Stablecoins got so big that governments started writing laws just for them.
scenes.p: Lawmakers in a grand hall study a giant green dollar coin under a huge magnifying glass, the wolf watching from the audience.

scenes.say: The main question: are they really backed one to one by safe assets?
Europe regulates them under MiCA. In 2025, the United States passed its own federal stablecoin law.
Rules usually require reserves, audits, and the right to redeem.
Clearer rules can make stablecoins safer, but they also decide who's allowed to issue them.
Follow for part 228: keeping records for taxes. Not financial advice.

228.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 228.

scenes.say: The tax office doesn't care that you forgot what you paid for your crypto.
scenes.p: The wolf sits at a desk buried under a mountain of messy receipts, looking lost, while a neat organized folder waits nearby.

scenes.say: In many countries, selling, swapping or spending crypto can be a taxable event.
You need the date, the amount, and the price of every buy and sell.
Export your exchange history regularly, before accounts close or data disappears.
Tax rules differ by country. Keep good records, and ask a local professional.
Follow for part 229: oil, the world's most traded commodity. Not financial advice.
One commodity moves the price of almost everything you buy: oil.
scenes.p: Black oil drops fall onto a big world map, each drop turning into tiny cars, planes and food packages.

scenes.say: It powers transport, plastics, chemicals and much of the world's energy.
Prices depend on supply from producers like the OPEC countries, and on global demand.
Wars, crises and recessions can send oil prices up or down very fast.
High oil prices feed inflation, which affects interest rates, stocks, and even crypto.
Follow for part 230: the four phases of a market cycle. Not financial advice.

230.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 230.

scenes.say: Markets move in cycles, with four classic phases.
scenes.p: A big circular road around a mountain passing through winter, spring, summer and autumn, the wolf walking along it.

scenes.say: Accumulation: prices are low and boring, and patient buyers quietly build positions.
Markup: prices rise, the trend becomes obvious, and more people join.
Distribution: prices stall near the top, while early buyers sell to late ones.
Markdown: prices fall and fear takes over, until the cycle starts again.
Follow for part 231: the Fear and Greed Index. Not financial advice.

231.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 231.

scenes.say: There's an index that measures the mood of the crypto market, from zero to one hundred.
scenes.p: A giant dial gauge going from a scared blue face to a greedy red face, the needle swinging, the wolf watching.

scenes.say: Low numbers mean extreme fear. High numbers mean extreme greed.
It mixes data like volatility, momentum, social media and search trends.
Extreme fear has often appeared near bottoms, and extreme greed near tops.
It's a mood check, not a timing tool. Moods can stay extreme for a long time.
Follow for part 232: commodities, explained. Not financial advice.
Commodities are the raw materials of the world: what we dig, drill and grow.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in a huge warehouse with sections for gold bars, oil barrels, wheat sacks and copper coils.

scenes.say: Energy like oil and gas, metals like gold and copper, and crops like wheat and coffee.
Their prices depend on supply, demand, the weather, and politics.
Many investors use ETFs for exposure, because trading futures is complex.
Commodities can protect against inflation, but they're volatile, and they pay no dividends.
Follow for part 233: buy the rumor, sell the news. Not financial advice.

233.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 233.

scenes.say: The big news finally came out, and the price dropped. Why?
scenes.p: The wolf reads a newspaper with a big happy front page while the chart behind him goes down, confused.

scenes.say: Traders buy in advance when an event is expected. The price rises on the rumor.
When the news actually happens, those traders take profit.
So good news that everyone expected can lead to a drop.
Always ask yourself: is this already priced in?
Follow for part 234: black swan events. Not financial advice.

234.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 234.

scenes.say: The events that hurt markets the most are the ones nobody saw coming.
scenes.p: A single black swan glides across a calm lake at night under the moon, the wolf watching from the shore.

scenes.say: They're called black swans: rare, unexpected, and with a huge impact.
The 2020 pandemic crash and the FTX collapse surprised almost everyone.
You can't predict them, but you can prepare: no leverage, diversification, and cash for emergencies.
Build a portfolio that survives the unexpected, not one that needs everything to go right.
Follow for part 235: why diamonds are a bad investment. Not financial advice.
Diamonds are forever. Their resale value isn't.
scenes.p: The wolf holds a big sparkling diamond ring at a pawn shop counter while the owner offers him one tiny coin for it.

scenes.say: When you buy a diamond, a big part of the price is the retail markup.
Selling it back usually gets you much less than you paid.
Lab-grown diamonds, chemically the same, have pushed prices down.
Buy diamonds because you love them, not as an investment.
Follow for part 236: the exchange listing effect. Not financial advice.

236.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 236.

scenes.say: A coin gets listed on a big exchange, and the price jumps. Then what?
scenes.p: A cartoon coin character walks onto a glamorous red carpet with flashing cameras and a cheering crowd, the wolf in the audience.

scenes.say: A new listing brings new buyers and more liquidity, so prices often spike.
Insiders and early holders often use that spike to sell.
Many coins fall back once the listing hype fades.
Chasing listing pumps is a fast game, usually won by those who got in early.
Follow for part 237: weekend volatility. Not financial advice.

237.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 237.

scenes.say: Crypto never closes. And weekends can get wild.
scenes.p: The wolf in pajamas on a Sunday morning stares at his phone showing a wild chart, a coffee cup in his other paw, surprised.

scenes.say: On weekends, many professional traders and institutions are off, so there's less liquidity.
With fewer orders on the book, smaller trades can move the price more.
Big moves on Sunday nights are common, as markets get ready for Monday.
If you trade on weekends, use smaller sizes and wider stops.
Follow for part 238: investing in art and collectibles. Not financial advice.
Paintings, watches, wine, trading cards. Can collectibles be real investments?
scenes.p: The wolf raises a paddle in a fancy auction house while the auctioneer lifts a gavel next to a framed painting.

scenes.say: Rare art, watches, wine, cards and classic cars can rise a lot in value.
But they're hard to sell quickly, and buying and selling costs can be very high.
You also pay for storage, insurance, and checking that they're authentic.
Collect what you love. Treat any profit as a bonus, not a plan.
Follow for part 239: companies that hold Bitcoin. Not financial advice.

239.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 239.

scenes.say: Some public companies hold billions of dollars in Bitcoin.
scenes.p: A tall corporate skyscraper with a giant golden Bitcoin on its roof, the wolf looking up from the street.

scenes.say: In 2020, the software company MicroStrategy, now called Strategy, started putting its cash into Bitcoin.
It kept buying, and now holds hundreds of thousands of bitcoin.
Tesla bought Bitcoin in 2021, and sold most of it the next year.
Their stocks give indirect Bitcoin exposure, often with extra risk from debt and company decisions.
Follow for part 240: El Salvador and Bitcoin. Not financial advice.

240.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 240.

scenes.say: One country tried to make Bitcoin everyday money.
scenes.p: A sunny Central American town square with palm trees and a big golden Bitcoin statue, the wolf wearing a straw hat.

scenes.say: In 2021, El Salvador became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender.
It launched a government wallet, and bought bitcoin for its treasury.
Everyday use stayed low, and in 2025, after a deal with the IMF, accepting Bitcoin became voluntary.
It's the biggest real-world experiment of Bitcoin as national money, and it's still being written.
Follow for part 241: real estate versus stocks. Not financial advice.
A house or the stock market? The eternal question.
scenes.p: The wolf stands between a cozy house on the left and a stock exchange building on the right, thinking with a paw on his chin.

scenes.say: Real estate lets you use a mortgage, so a small deposit controls a big asset.
It can pay rent, but it takes work and money for repairs, and it's hard to sell fast.
Stocks are easy to buy in small amounts and sell in seconds, but prices swing every day.
Over the long run, both have built wealth. Many people own some of each.
Follow for part 242: the biggest lessons so far, part two. Not financial advice.

242.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 242.

scenes.say: Time for another look back at the biggest lessons so far.
scenes.p: The wolf flips through a photo album of his past adventures by a fireplace, smiling, warm light.

scenes.say: Security first: your seed phrase is everything, and real support never asks for it.
Most scams promise fixed high returns, or rush you. Slow down, and verify.
Know what you own: the supply, the unlocks, and who holds the coins.
Emotions are the enemy: fear, greed and FOMO. A written plan is the cure.
Follow for part 243: Bitcoin mining and energy. Not financial advice.

243.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 243.

scenes.say: Bitcoin mining uses a huge amount of energy. Is that a problem?
scenes.p: A giant Bitcoin mining farm next to a waterfall and a hydroelectric dam, the wolf in a hard hat.

scenes.say: Bitcoin mining uses about as much electricity as some entire countries.
Critics call it wasteful. Supporters say it secures a global monetary network.
Miners chase the cheapest power, so many use surplus, stranded or renewable energy.
The debate continues, and it shapes how governments regulate mining.
Follow for part 244: GDP, explained. Not financial advice.
You hear about GDP on the news all the time. Here's what it actually means.
scenes.p: The wolf stands on top of a giant growing bar chart made of factories, shops and houses, holding a flag.

scenes.say: GDP, gross domestic product, is the total value of everything a country produces in a year.
When GDP grows, companies usually earn more, and jobs are easier to find.
When it shrinks for a while, the economy is in a recession.
Markets react to GDP news, but stock prices often move before the economy does.
Follow for part 245: hashrate, explained. Not financial advice.

245.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 245.

scenes.say: There's one number that shows how strongly Bitcoin is protected: the hashrate.
scenes.p: A giant glowing speedometer made of mining machines, its needle racing upward, the wolf amazed.

scenes.say: Hashrate measures how much computing power is securing a proof of work network like Bitcoin.
Higher hashrate means more miners, and a network that's harder to attack.
About every two weeks, Bitcoin adjusts the mining difficulty, to keep blocks coming roughly every ten minutes.
Hashrate has kept rising over the years, a sign of miners' long-term confidence.
Follow for part 246: yield farming. Not financial advice.

246.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 246.

scenes.say: Farming, but for crypto. Here's how yield farming works.
scenes.p: The wolf as a farmer in overalls over his suit harvests glowing coins from neat rows of crypto plants in a futuristic field.

scenes.say: Yield farming means moving your crypto into DeFi apps to earn rewards.
You might provide liquidity, lend, or stake, and earn fees plus extra tokens.
Those reward tokens can lose value fast, wiping out the yield.
Add smart contract risk on top. High yields usually mean high risk.
Follow for part 247: recessions. Not financial advice.
Everyone fears the word recession. Here's what it really is.
scenes.p: A city street in the rain with closed shops and a long line of people, the wolf holding an umbrella.

scenes.say: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity that lasts for months.
A common rule of thumb is two quarters in a row of shrinking GDP.
Companies earn less, unemployment rises, and stocks often fall before and during it.
But recessions end. Investors who keep buying during them often benefit in the recovery.
Follow for part 248: APY versus APR. Not financial advice.

248.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 248.

scenes.say: Same deal, two different numbers. APY versus APR.
scenes.p: The wolf compares two glowing shop window signs showing different percentage symbols, holding a magnifying glass.

scenes.say: APR is the simple yearly rate, without compounding.
APY includes compounding: earning interest on your interest.
The same deal looks bigger in APY, so some platforms advertise APY on purpose.
Compare the same kind of number, and always ask where the yield actually comes from.
Follow for part 249: when a yield is too good to be true. Not financial advice.

249.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 249.

scenes.say: If a yield looks too good to be true, ask one question: where does it come from?
scenes.p: A shiny carnival stand advertising a giant glowing percentage sign with balloons, a trap door hidden in front of it, the wolf stopping just in time.

scenes.say: Real yields come from somewhere: borrowers paying interest, trading fees, or network rewards.
If you can't find the source, you might be the source.
In 2022, platforms promising high, safe yields, like Celsius and Anchor, collapsed.
A risk-free twenty percent is usually neither risk-free, nor really twenty percent.
Follow for part 250: what central banks do. Not financial advice.
A few people in a few buildings can move every market on Earth. Central banks.
scenes.p: A grand central bank building with tall columns and a giant golden key above the entrance, the wolf on the steps.

scenes.say: A central bank, like the Federal Reserve or the European Central Bank, manages a currency.
It sets key interest rates, and tries to keep inflation under control.
In a crisis, it can lend to banks and create new money.
Its decisions move stocks, bonds, currencies and crypto. That's why markets hang on every word.
Follow for part 251: crypto lending and collateral. Not financial advice.

251.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 251.

scenes.say: You can borrow money without selling your crypto. But there's a catch.
scenes.p: The wolf hands a big golden coin to a robot pawnbroker behind glass and receives a smaller stack of green dollar coins.

scenes.say: In crypto lending, you lock up crypto as collateral, and borrow against it.
Loans are usually over-collateralized: you deposit more value than you borrow.
If your collateral's price falls too much, it gets sold automatically to repay the loan.
Borrow conservatively, or not at all. Volatility won't wait for you to add more collateral.
Follow for part 252: liquidations in DeFi. Not financial advice.

252.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 252.

scenes.say: In DeFi, nobody calls you before selling your collateral.
scenes.p: A glowing robotic auctioneer instantly sells a pile of the wolf's coins while a red alarm flashes, the wolf running toward it too late.

scenes.say: There's no margin call. Smart contracts liquidate loans automatically.
When a loan's health drops below a threshold, others can repay part of it, and take your collateral at a discount.
In fast crashes, many positions get liquidated at once, pushing prices even lower.
Keep a big safety margin, and watch your loan's health factor.
Follow for part 253: interest rates, explained. Not financial advice.
One number affects your mortgage, your savings, and the price of your crypto: the interest rate.
scenes.p: A giant golden dial with a lever controls the flow of money from a big pipe into a city, the wolf turning it.

scenes.say: An interest rate is the price of money: what borrowers pay, and what savers earn.
Low rates make borrowing cheap, which encourages spending and investing.
High rates cool the economy, and make safe savings more attractive than risky assets.
That's why rate changes ripple through stocks, bonds, real estate and crypto.
Follow for part 254: flash loans. Not financial advice.

254.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 254.

scenes.say: Borrow millions with no collateral, and pay it back in the same second. That's a flash loan.
scenes.p: The wolf borrows a mountain of gold coins and returns it in the same blink of an eye, a bright lightning flash, comic style.

scenes.say: A flash loan lets you borrow huge amounts with no collateral, if you repay it in the same transaction.
If it isn't repaid, the whole transaction is canceled, as if it never happened.
Traders use them for arbitrage. Attackers have used them to manipulate prices and exploit protocols.
For regular users, the lesson is simple: use protocols that are audited and battle-tested.
Follow for part 255: DAOs. Not financial advice.

255.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 255.

scenes.say: What if a company had no CEO, and token holders made the decisions?
scenes.p: A big round glowing table in a futuristic hall where many different people vote by raising glowing tokens, the wolf among them.

scenes.say: That's a DAO: a decentralized autonomous organization, run through smart contracts and token votes.
Members propose changes and vote, and the code executes the result.
In 2016, a famous DAO was hacked, which led to a split of Ethereum.
DAOs can be powerful, but votes are often controlled by a few big holders.
Follow for part 256: money printing and quantitative easing. Not financial advice.
When a crisis hits, central banks can create money out of thin air.
scenes.p: A giant money printing press running at full speed with banknotes flying everywhere, the wolf watching with a cup of coffee.

scenes.say: In 2008 and 2020, central banks created money on a massive scale.
With quantitative easing, they buy bonds, pushing money into the system and lowering long-term rates.
Asset prices often rise: stocks, real estate, and crypto.
The side effects can include inflation and bubbles. There's no free lunch.
Follow for part 257: governance tokens. Not financial advice.

257.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 257.

scenes.say: Some tokens give you a vote. They're called governance tokens.
scenes.p: The wolf drops a glowing token into a futuristic ballot box while other people wait in line to vote behind him.

scenes.say: Holders vote on how a protocol changes.
Fees, rewards, upgrades, treasury spending: holders decide.
But many governance tokens have little direct claim on revenue, so their value is debated.
And when a few wallets hold most of the votes, decentralization is mostly a story.
Follow for part 258: liquid staking. Not financial advice.

258.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 258.

scenes.say: Staking usually locks your coins. Liquid staking gives you a receipt you can still use.
scenes.p: The wolf locks gold coins in a glowing vault and receives a shiny ticket that also glows like a coin, smiling.

scenes.say: You stake your ether, for example, and receive a token that represents your staked coins.
You keep earning staking rewards, and you can trade or use that token in DeFi.
The risk: that token can trade below the real value in a panic.
And you add the risk of the liquid staking platform itself. More layers, more risk.
Follow for part 259: the US dollar as the world's currency. Not financial advice.
Why does almost the whole world trade in US dollars?
scenes.p: A giant green dollar coin sits at the center of a globe with ships, planes and pipelines all connected to it, the wolf pointing.

scenes.say: Oil, many commodities and much of global trade are priced in dollars.
Central banks hold dollars as their main reserve currency.
That gives the US huge financial power, and makes the dollar a safe haven in crises.
When the dollar gets stronger, it often puts pressure on stocks, commodities and crypto.
Follow for part 260: restaking and its risks. Not financial advice.

260.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 260.

scenes.say: Restaking: earning more by using the same staked coins again. What could go wrong?
scenes.p: The wolf stacks the same glowing coin on top of several pedestals at once like a juggling act, the tower wobbling.

scenes.say: With restaking, staked ether is used to secure extra services, for extra rewards.
But the same collateral now backs several promises at once.
If something fails, penalties can hit your stake in more than one place.
More yield, more layers, more risk. Understand it before chasing it.
Follow for part 261: tokenized real-world assets. Not financial advice.

261.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 261.

scenes.say: Bonds, buildings and gold on a blockchain? That's tokenization.
scenes.p: A building, a gold bar and a bond certificate being scanned into glowing digital tokens by a futuristic machine, the wolf operating it.

scenes.say: Tokenized real-world assets are tokens that represent ownership of things like treasury bills or real estate.
Big financial firms have launched tokenized funds, especially for government bonds.
Benefits: faster settlement, trading around the clock, and small minimum amounts.
But you still depend on the company holding the real asset, and on the law.
Follow for part 262: forex basics. Not financial advice.
The biggest market in the world isn't stocks or crypto. It's currencies.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a huge glowing board of currency symbols changing at high speed in a busy trading room.

scenes.say: Forex is the trading of currencies, like euros against dollars, every weekday, around the clock.
Exchange rates move with interest rates, trade, and the economy.
Moves are usually small, so forex traders often use high leverage.
And that leverage is why most retail forex traders lose money.
Follow for part 263: MEV and front-running. Not financial advice.

263.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 263.

scenes.say: Sometimes someone sees your crypto trade before it happens, and profits from it.
scenes.p: A shadowy figure with binoculars spies on a queue of glowing transaction envelopes and cuts in front of the line, the wolf frowning.

scenes.say: On public blockchains, pending transactions wait in a public queue.
Bots can see a big trade coming, jump ahead of it, and profit from the price move. That's called MEV.
Users pay through worse prices, without noticing.
Use tight slippage settings and wallets that offer protected transaction routes.
Follow for part 264: the different types of wallets. Not financial advice.

264.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 264.

scenes.say: Not all wallets are the same. Here are the main types.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a display case showing a phone, a laptop, a small hardware device and a metal plate, like a museum guide.

scenes.say: Exchange wallets: easy, but the exchange holds your keys.
Mobile and browser wallets: you hold the keys, on a device connected to the internet.
Hardware wallets: keys stay offline, on a small device. Great for savings.
Many people use a mix: a little on mobile, most offline.
Follow for part 265: unemployment and the economy. Not financial advice.
Strangely, bad news for jobs can be good news for markets. Here's why.
scenes.p: A long line of people waiting outside a job center while the wolf reads a newspaper with a surprised face.

scenes.say: The unemployment rate shows how many people want a job but can't find one.
Rising unemployment can signal a slowing economy, and lower profits.
But it can also push central banks to cut rates, which markets often like.
Markets care about what happens next, not just the number itself.
Follow for part 266: crypto-backed stablecoins. Not financial advice.

266.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 266.

scenes.say: A stablecoin with no bank behind it, backed only by crypto. How does that work?
scenes.p: A glowing vault full of gold coins with a smaller stack of green dollar coins coming out of a slot, the wolf supervising.

scenes.say: Crypto-backed stablecoins, like DAI, are created when users lock more crypto than they borrow.
For example, you lock one hundred fifty dollars of ether to mint one hundred dollars of stablecoins.
If the collateral falls too much, it's liquidated to keep the stablecoin backed.
No bank needed, but a big crash can test the whole system.
Follow for part 267: algorithmic stablecoins. Not financial advice.

267.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 267.

scenes.say: A stablecoin with no real reserves, kept at one dollar by an algorithm. Sounds risky? It is.
scenes.p: A green dollar coin balanced on top of a fragile tower of gears and springs, the wolf watching nervously.

scenes.say: Algorithmic stablecoins try to hold their price with code and a second token.
It works while people trust it. When confidence breaks, it can spiral down.
TerraUSD collapsed in May 2022, wiping out tens of billions of dollars.
If a stablecoin's backing is just confidence, treat it as a risky asset.
Follow for part 268: the inverted yield curve. Not financial advice.
This chart has warned of several US recessions. It's called the inverted yield curve.
scenes.p: A glowing curved road that suddenly flips upside down like a loop, a car with the wolf driving carefully toward it.

scenes.say: Normally, long-term bonds pay more than short-term ones. You get paid for waiting.
When short-term rates rise above long-term ones, the curve is inverted.
It often means markets expect rates, and growth, to fall in the future.
It has a good track record as a warning, but timing is unreliable. Recessions can come years later, or not at all.
Follow for part 269: NFT royalties and utility. Not financial advice.

269.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 269.

scenes.say: NFTs aren't only pictures. Some come with royalties, and real utility.
scenes.p: A glowing digital ticket and a game sword float above the wolf's open paw in a neon gallery.

scenes.say: Royalties let creators earn a share every time their NFT is resold, if the marketplace enforces it.
Many marketplaces made royalties optional, which hurt creators.
Utility can mean event tickets, game items, memberships, or proof of ownership.
Utility can add value, but only if people actually want what it unlocks.
Follow for part 270: play-to-earn: the boom and the bust. Not financial advice.

270.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 270.

scenes.say: Play games, earn money. In 2021, it sounded like the future.
scenes.p: The wolf plays a colorful video game on a big screen while coins pour out of it, then the coins turn to dust.

scenes.say: Games like Axie Infinity let players earn tokens, and some made a living from it.
But rewards were paid by new players buying in.
When new players slowed, token prices collapsed, and so did the earnings.
A game has to be fun without the money. Otherwise, the economy eats itself.
Follow for part 271: stagflation. Not financial advice.
High inflation and a weak economy at the same time. That's stagflation.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in a gloomy city where prices balloons rise into the sky while factories stand still and grey.

scenes.say: Usually, a weak economy brings lower inflation. In stagflation, prices keep rising anyway.
The 1970s are the classic example, with oil shocks and rising unemployment.
It's hard to fight: raising rates hurts growth, cutting rates feeds inflation.
Historically, stocks and bonds both struggled, while commodities often did better.
Follow for part 272: the metaverse hype cycle. Not financial advice.

272.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 272.

scenes.say: In 2021, everyone was buying virtual land in the metaverse.
scenes.p: The wolf in VR goggles stands on a floating plot of glowing virtual land with a for-sale sign, in a pixelated world.

scenes.say: Virtual plots and metaverse tokens sold for huge amounts.
Big companies rushed in, and the hype peaked within months.
Then users didn't show up, and many metaverse tokens fell more than ninety percent.
Hype cycles repeat. The technology may survive, while early prices don't.
Follow for part 273: narratives and sector rotation. Not financial advice.

273.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 273.

scenes.say: In crypto, money moves in waves from one story to the next. They're called narratives.
scenes.p: Waves of glowing coins surfing from one island to another, each island with a different theme, the wolf on a surfboard.

scenes.say: DeFi, NFTs, AI tokens, memes: each cycle has its hot themes.
Money rotates fast, and early movers profit the most.
Late buyers often enter just as the money is leaving.
Understanding narratives helps. Chasing every one usually doesn't.
Follow for part 274: hyperinflation. Not financial advice.
Imagine a wheelbarrow full of cash that can't buy a loaf of bread. That's hyperinflation.
scenes.p: The wolf pushes a wheelbarrow overflowing with banknotes to a bakery to buy a single loaf of bread.

scenes.say: Hyperinflation is when prices rise extremely fast, often more than fifty percent a month.
Germany in the 1920s, Zimbabwe in the 2000s, and Venezuela more recently are famous examples.
It usually comes from massive money printing and a loss of trust in the currency.
In those moments, people run to anything that holds value: dollars, gold, and sometimes crypto.
Follow for part 275: airdrop farming. Not financial advice.

275.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 275.

scenes.say: Some people use crypto apps every day just to qualify for future airdrops.
scenes.p: The wolf clicks through many glowing apps on several phones, a big parachute gift floating in the distance.

scenes.say: Airdrop farming means using new protocols early, hoping to receive free tokens later.
Some farmers earned a lot. Many spent more on fees and time than they got back.
Projects now filter out fake accounts and bots, so rules keep changing.
Never connect to fake airdrop sites. Most free tokens offered by strangers are traps.
Follow for part 276: how much should you invest. Not financial advice.

276.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 276.

scenes.say: How much should you invest in crypto? There's no magic number, but there are good rules.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a big pie made of coins, holding a knife and thinking how big a slice to cut.

scenes.say: First, have an emergency fund, and no expensive debt.
Then only invest money you could lose without changing your life.
Many people keep crypto to a small percentage of their total savings.
Start small, learn, and only grow it if you can handle the swings.
Follow for part 277: tulip mania. Not financial advice.
In the 1630s, a single tulip bulb reportedly sold for the price of a house.
scenes.p: A beautiful red tulip in a pot on a velvet pedestal in an old Dutch market, a crowd of people in 1600s clothes bidding.

scenes.say: It's called tulip mania, in the Dutch Republic, and it's one of the most famous bubbles in history.
Prices rose as people bought tulips just to sell them higher.
In early 1637, buyers suddenly disappeared, and prices collapsed.
The details are debated, but the lesson isn't: when price is only about hype, it can vanish fast.
Follow for part 278: is it too late to buy Bitcoin. Not financial advice.

278.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 278.

scenes.say: People asked if it was too late to buy Bitcoin at ten dollars, at a thousand, and at fifty thousand.
scenes.p: The wolf looks at a long train with a golden Bitcoin on the front already leaving the station, while people on the platform shout and wave.

scenes.say: Nobody knows the future price. Anyone who claims to know is guessing.
The better question: does Bitcoin have a place in your long-term plan, and how big?
If yes, many people build a position slowly, instead of all at once.
It's never too late for a careful decision. It's always too late to undo a reckless one.
Follow for part 279: can crypto go to zero. Not financial advice.

279.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 279.

scenes.say: Can crypto go to zero? Some coins already have. Thousands of them.
scenes.p: A huge abandoned junkyard of rusty broken coins under a grey sky, the wolf walking through it with a flashlight.

scenes.say: Most small coins fail: no users, no developers, or outright scams.
Bitcoin has been declared dead hundreds of times by the media, and has survived so far.
Surviving so far isn't a guarantee, so size every position as if it could fail.
Spread out, favor the strongest projects, and never bet what you can't afford to lose.
Follow for part 280: the South Sea bubble. Not financial advice.
Even Isaac Newton couldn't resist a bubble.
scenes.p: An elegant 1700s London coffee house full of men in wigs shouting and waving stock papers, the wolf in a period costume watching.

scenes.say: In 1720, shares of Britain's South Sea Company soared on promises of trade riches.
Everyone wanted in: nobles, merchants, even scientists.
Then the bubble burst, and fortunes vanished. Newton reportedly lost a lot of money.
Smart people aren't immune to hype. That's why rules matter more than intelligence.
Follow for part 281: what to do after a big loss. Not financial advice.

281.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 281.

scenes.say: You just lost a lot of money. What now?
scenes.p: The wolf sits on the floor leaning against a wall in a dim room, head down, a single ray of sunlight coming through the window.

scenes.say: First, don't try to win it back fast. That's how losses get bigger.
Take a break. Then write down exactly what happened, and why.
Was it the plan, the position size, or your emotions? Find the real lesson.
Losses are expensive lessons. Make sure you pay for each one only once.
Follow for part 282: your first purchase, step by step. Not financial advice.

282.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 282.

scenes.say: Your first crypto purchase, step by step.
scenes.p: The wolf carefully crosses a river on a path of glowing stepping stones, one careful step at a time.

scenes.say: One: pick a regulated, well-known exchange, and turn on two-factor authentication.
Two: verify your identity, and deposit a small amount from your bank.
Three: buy with a limit order, and double-check the amount before you confirm.
Four: decide whether to keep it there or move it to your own wallet. Start small, and learn.
Follow for part 283: the Great Depression. Not financial advice.
In 1929, a stock market crash started the worst economic crisis of the modern era.
scenes.p: A 1929 street scene with a crowd of worried people in hats outside a bank with closed doors, the wolf among them in vintage clothes.

scenes.say: From its 1929 peak to 1932, the Dow Jones lost almost ninety percent.
Banks failed, unemployment soared, and savings disappeared.
It took about twenty-five years for the Dow to get back to its 1929 high.
It's why we have deposit insurance today, and why central banks act fast in a crisis.
Follow for part 284: how to cash out to your bank. Not financial advice.

284.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 284.

scenes.say: Making money in crypto is one thing. Getting it into your bank account is another.
scenes.p: The wolf walks across a bridge from a glowing crypto city to a classic bank building, carrying a bag of coins.

scenes.say: Usually, you sell on an exchange for your local currency, then withdraw to your bank.
Use the same name and bank account you verified, to avoid delays.
Big withdrawals may trigger checks. Keep records showing where the money came from.
And taxes may apply when you sell. Plan before you cash out.
Follow for part 285: recurring buys. Not financial advice.

285.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 285.

scenes.say: The easiest investing strategy runs on autopilot.
scenes.p: The wolf relaxes in a lounge chair while a little robot drops one gold coin into a jar every week next to a calendar.

scenes.say: A recurring buy purchases a fixed amount automatically, every week or every month.
You stop trying to time the market, and you stop forgetting.
Over time, you buy more when prices are low, and less when they're high.
Check the fees, and pick an amount you can keep up for years.
Follow for part 286: Black Monday 1987. Not financial advice.
On October 19th, 1987, the Dow Jones fell almost twenty-three percent in a single day.
scenes.p: A 1980s trading floor in total chaos, traders in big suits throwing papers, old computer screens glowing red, the wolf in an 80s suit.

scenes.say: It's still the Dow's biggest one-day percentage drop ever.
Computer-driven selling and panic fed on each other.
Yet the market recovered those losses within about two years.
Crashes feel endless while they happen. History says patience usually wins.
Follow for part 287: price alerts. Not financial advice.

287.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 287.

scenes.say: Stop staring at charts. Let them call you.
scenes.p: The wolf relaxes on a sofa reading a book while his phone on the table lights up with a gentle bell alert.

scenes.say: A price alert notifies you when a coin hits a level you choose.
Set alerts at your entry zones, your targets, and your stop levels.
Then close the app, and live your life.
Alerts are for decisions you already planned, not for panic.
Follow for part 288: tracking your portfolio. Not financial advice.

288.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 288.

scenes.say: Do you know how much you actually own across all your exchanges and wallets?
scenes.p: The wolf looks at a big glowing dashboard that combines several wallets and exchanges into one clear pie chart.

scenes.say: A portfolio tracker, or a simple spreadsheet, shows everything in one place.
Track your total value, your allocation, and what you paid.
Use read-only connections. Never give a tracker the power to trade or withdraw.
Review it monthly, not every hour.
Follow for part 289: the dot-com bubble. Not financial advice.
In the late 1990s, any company with dot com in its name could double overnight.
scenes.p: A 1999 office full of bean bags, computers and confetti, a giant bubble with a computer mouse inside inflating above, the wolf in a casual shirt.

scenes.say: Investors poured money into internet startups with no profits.
In March 2000 the Nasdaq peaked. By 2002, it had lost almost eighty percent.
Many companies vanished. A few, like Amazon, survived and became giants.
The internet was real. The prices weren't. Great technology doesn't always mean a good price.
Follow for part 290: rebalancing, with a real example. Not financial advice.

290.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 290.

scenes.say: Your plan was half Bitcoin, half stablecoins. Then Bitcoin doubled. Now what?
scenes.p: The wolf adjusts a big balance scale tipped heavily to the golden side, moving some coins to the green side.

scenes.say: Now about two thirds of your money is in Bitcoin. Your risk has quietly grown.
Rebalancing means selling some of the winner, to get back to your target.
It forces you to take profit when prices are high, and buy when they're low.
Do it on a schedule, or when your mix drifts too far. Not on feelings.
Follow for part 291: taking profit into stablecoins or cash. Not financial advice.

291.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 291.

scenes.say: You took profit. Where do you park it?
scenes.p: The wolf drives a car full of gold coins into a garage with two lanes: one leading to a green coin vault, the other to a bank.

scenes.say: Stablecoins keep you in crypto, ready to buy again, but carry issuer and platform risk.
Cash in your bank leaves crypto completely, and usually has stronger protection.
Remember that selling may be taxable, whichever you choose.
Many people do both: some cash to secure gains, some stablecoins for opportunities.
Follow for part 292: the 2008 financial crisis. Not financial advice.
In 2008, a crisis in American home loans nearly brought down the global financial system.
scenes.p: A row of suburban houses made of playing cards collapses one after another, giant bank towers wobbling behind them, the wolf shocked.

scenes.say: Banks had lent to people who couldn't repay, then packaged those loans into complex products.
When house prices fell, losses spread everywhere. Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008.
From peak to bottom, the S&P 500 lost more than half its value.
Governments and central banks stepped in massively. And just months later, Bitcoin was born.
Follow for part 293: when to sell: your reason is gone. Not financial advice.

293.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 293.

scenes.say: When should you sell? When the reason you bought is gone.
scenes.p: The wolf looks at a broken lightbulb on his desk next to a crossed-out note, deciding what to do.

scenes.say: Before buying, write down why: the team, the technology, the trend, the valuation.
If that reason breaks, the team leaves, the tech fails, the story changes, it's time to reconsider.
A falling price alone isn't a reason. A broken thesis is.
Selling because the story changed is discipline, not weakness.
Follow for part 294: HODL, and where it comes from. Not financial advice.

294.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 294.

scenes.say: In December 2013, a Bitcoin fan posted on a forum, with a typo: I AM HODLING.
scenes.p: The wolf laughs at an old computer screen in a dark room at night, a forum page glowing with a funny message.

scenes.say: He meant holding. The typo became one of crypto's most famous words.
HODL now means holding through crashes, instead of panic selling.
It worked for some long-term holders, but holding a bad coin forever is not a strategy.
Hold what you believe in, for reasons you can explain.
Follow for part 295: the 2020 COVID crash. Not financial advice.
In March 2020, markets fell faster than ever before.
scenes.p: Empty city streets with people in masks and a giant red falling arrow across the sky, the wolf wearing a mask.

scenes.say: The S&P 500 dropped about a third in roughly a month.
Bitcoin fell around half in just two days.
Then central banks and governments flooded the system with money.
By August, the S&P 500 was at new highs. Those who panic sold missed the recovery.
Follow for part 296: diamond hands versus paper hands. Not financial advice.

296.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 296.

scenes.say: Diamond hands or paper hands? Crypto's favorite insult, explained.
scenes.p: Two cartoon hands: one sparkling diamond hand holding a coin tightly, one crumpled paper hand dropping its coin, the wolf between them.

scenes.say: Diamond hands means holding through brutal drops, no matter what.
Paper hands means selling at the first sign of trouble.
Neither is always right. Holding a failing project isn't strength.
Real strength is following your plan: hold when it says hold, sell when it says sell.
Follow for part 297: DYOR: do your own research. Not financial advice.

297.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 297.

scenes.say: Do your own research. Everyone says it. Few people actually do it.
scenes.p: The wolf sits at a library table piled with books, papers, a laptop and a magnifying glass, deeply focused.

scenes.say: Research means reading the project's documents, not just posts about it.
Check the team, the tokenomics, the users, and the risks.
Look for critics, not just fans.
If you can't explain why you own something, you did someone else's research, not yours.
Follow for part 298: Japan's lost decades. Not financial advice.
Japan's stock market peaked in 1989, and took thirty-four years to get back there.
scenes.p: A Tokyo skyline in 1989 with neon lights and a giant golden peak, then the wolf as an old man waiting on a bench under cherry blossoms.

scenes.say: In the late 1980s, Japanese stocks and real estate were in a giant bubble.
Then it burst, and the Nikkei index lost most of its value.
It only returned to its 1989 high in 2024.
The lesson: buying at the peak of a bubble can take decades to recover, even in a great economy.
Follow for part 299: ATH and ATL. Not financial advice.

299.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 299.

scenes.say: ATH, ATL. Two abbreviations you'll see everywhere in crypto.
scenes.p: The wolf stands on the top of a very high mountain peak with a flag, and far below him a deep valley in shadow.

scenes.say: ATH means all-time high: the highest price ever reached.
ATL means all-time low: the lowest price ever.
New all-time highs often attract new buyers, and lots of hype.
Remember: a coin far below its ATH isn't automatically cheap. It might never return there.
Follow for part 300: myth: crypto is only for criminals. Not financial advice.

300.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 300.

scenes.say: Myth: crypto is only for criminals. Let's look at the facts.
scenes.p: The wolf as a detective holds a magnifying glass over a giant pile of coins where only a tiny few have a dark shadow.

scenes.say: Blockchain analysis firms estimate that illicit activity is a small share of crypto transactions, around one percent or less.
And most blockchains are public, so criminals can be traced. Many have been caught.
Cash is still the favorite tool for crime around the world.
Crypto has risks, and scams are real. But most users are regular people.
Follow for part 301: crypto versus stocks: the real differences. Not financial advice.
Crypto and stocks both have charts. That's where the similarities end.
scenes.p: A split scene: on the left a calm classic stock exchange, on the right a wild neon crypto city, the wolf standing on the dividing line.

scenes.say: A stock is a share of a company with profits, assets and legal rights.
Most crypto tokens don't give you ownership or dividends. Value comes from use and demand.
Crypto trades every second of every day, and moves much more.
Different tools, different risks. Know which game you're playing.
Follow for part 302: myth: you need a lot of money to start. Not financial advice.

302.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 302.

scenes.say: Myth: you need a lot of money to start investing.
scenes.p: The wolf drops a single small coin into a big empty jar, smiling, as a tiny sprout grows next to it.

scenes.say: Most crypto apps and many brokers let you start with a few dollars or euros.
Fractional shares let you buy pieces of expensive stocks.
Starting small is actually smart: you learn while your mistakes are cheap.
The habit matters more than the amount.
Follow for part 303: myth: a cheap coin will easily 100x. Not financial advice.

303.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 303.

scenes.say: Myth: a coin that costs a fraction of a cent can easily go up a hundred times.
scenes.p: A tiny penny coin stands on a stage trying to wear a giant crown that's far too big for it, the wolf laughing.

scenes.say: A low price usually means there are billions or trillions of coins.
To go up a hundred times, its total value must grow a hundred times too.
That often means reaching valuations bigger than the largest companies on Earth.
Check the market cap, not the price tag.
Follow for part 304: stock market hours versus crypto's 24/7. Not financial advice.
The stock market sleeps. Crypto never does.
scenes.p: Half of the image shows a stock exchange building at night with its doors closed, the other half a glowing crypto city wide awake, the wolf yawning between them.

scenes.say: Most stock exchanges trade on weekdays, during set hours.
Crypto trades twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays.
That means big crypto moves can happen while you sleep.
Use stop losses and alerts, and never risk more than you can sleep with.
Follow for part 305: myth: crypto is just a Ponzi scheme. Not financial advice.

305.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 305.

scenes.say: Myth: crypto is just a giant Ponzi scheme. Is it?
scenes.p: The wolf as a judge with a gavel examines two exhibits on a table: a fragile tower of people and a glowing blockchain.

scenes.say: A Ponzi pays old investors with new investors' money, and hides it.
Bitcoin has no company promising returns. Its rules and transactions are public.
But many crypto projects have been Ponzis, promising fixed returns from nowhere.
So the honest answer: some crypto is a scam. The technology itself isn't.
Follow for part 306: myth: Bitcoin is anonymous. Not financial advice.

306.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 306.

scenes.say: Myth: Bitcoin is anonymous. Actually, it's one of the most traceable forms of money.
scenes.p: The wolf follows a glowing trail of footprints made of coins across a digital landscape with a magnifying glass.

scenes.say: Every transaction is public and permanent on the blockchain.
Addresses don't show names, but exchanges know who you are.
Analysis firms link addresses to people every day.
Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous. Act accordingly.
Follow for part 307: AI stocks and the hype. Not financial advice.
AI is changing the world. Does that make every AI stock a good investment?
scenes.p: A friendly robot stands on top of a rocket made of stock certificates, a crowd cheering below, the wolf watching carefully.

scenes.say: Chip makers and big tech companies have gained hugely from the AI boom.
Many small companies just add AI to their name, and their price jumps.
The dot-com era showed that real technology can still create bubbles.
Look for real revenue and profits, not just the buzzword.
Follow for part 308: the 2016 DAO hack. Not financial advice.

308.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 308.

scenes.say: In 2016, an Ethereum project raised a fortune, and lost a big part of it to a hacker.
scenes.p: A giant glowing vault with a tiny crack in its code wall, a shadowy figure pulling ether coins out through the crack.

scenes.say: It was called The DAO, a fund run by smart contracts and token votes.
A bug let an attacker drain millions of ether.
The Ethereum community split the chain to return the funds. The old chain became Ethereum Classic.
Code can have bugs. Big money in new smart contracts means big risk.
Follow for part 309: the 2017 ICO boom. Not financial advice.

309.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 309.

scenes.say: In 2017, a whitepaper and a website could raise millions in days. Welcome to the ICO boom.
scenes.p: A crowd throws money at a stage where a presenter shows a glowing whitepaper, the wolf watching skeptically.

scenes.say: ICO means initial coin offering: selling new tokens directly to the public.
Projects raised billions of dollars, often with no product.
Most of those tokens later lost almost all their value, and many were outright scams.
Regulators cracked down, and the lesson stuck: a whitepaper is not a business.
Follow for part 310: Tesla and volatile stocks. Not financial advice.
Some stocks move like crypto. Tesla is the famous example.
scenes.p: A bright red electric sports car on a giant roller coaster track shaped like a wild stock chart, the wolf driving.

scenes.say: Tesla became one of the most valuable companies in the world.
But its stock has also fallen more than sixty percent in a single year.
Prices like that reflect huge expectations about the future.
If you own volatile stocks, size them like you'd size crypto.
Follow for part 311: DeFi summer. Not financial advice.

311.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 311.

scenes.say: In the summer of 2020, decentralized finance exploded. It was called DeFi summer.
scenes.p: A sunny beach party where glowing coins grow on palm trees and people swim in a pool of tokens, the wolf with sunglasses.

scenes.say: Lending apps started rewarding users with governance tokens, and yield farming was born.
Decentralized exchanges boomed, and Uniswap gave free tokens to its early users.
Yields reached crazy levels, and new tokens launched every day.
Some projects became pillars of DeFi. Many others disappeared within months.
Follow for part 312: the 2021 NFT mania. Not financial advice.

312.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 312.

scenes.say: In 2021, a digital artwork sold for sixty-nine million dollars. The NFT mania had begun.
scenes.p: A grand auction hall where an auctioneer bangs a gavel next to a glowing digital artwork on a screen, the crowd gasping.

scenes.say: Cartoon apes and pixel avatars became status symbols, selling for hundreds of thousands.
Celebrities bought in, and new collections sold out in minutes.
Then trading volume collapsed, and most NFTs lost almost all their value.
Manias always feel permanent from the inside.
Follow for part 313: brand value as an investment. Not financial advice.
Why do people pay more for a logo? Brand value is one of the strongest investments.
scenes.p: The wolf stands in front of a shop with a long line of people waiting to buy a product, holding a shopping bag.

scenes.say: Strong brands can charge higher prices, because customers trust them.
That means higher profit margins, year after year.
Brands like Apple, Coca-Cola or luxury fashion houses have defended their prices for decades.
But brands can fade. Watch whether customers stay loyal, not just the logo.
Follow for part 314: the Terra Luna collapse. Not financial advice.

314.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 314.

scenes.say: In May 2022, a top-ten crypto collapsed in days. Terra Luna.
scenes.p: A giant moon cracks and crumbles into dust in the night sky, the wolf watching from a rooftop in shock.

scenes.say: TerraUSD was an algorithmic stablecoin, linked to the Luna token.
A lending app called Anchor paid around twenty percent on it, attracting billions.
When confidence broke, the stablecoin lost its peg, and Luna fell to almost zero.
Tens of billions of dollars vanished, and its founder later faced criminal charges.
Follow for part 315: the lessons of the FTX collapse. Not financial advice.

315.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 315.

scenes.say: FTX was one of the biggest exchanges in the world. In November 2022, it collapsed in days.
scenes.p: A huge glamorous exchange tower with spotlights crumbling into a pile of bricks, the wolf watching from the street in shock.

scenes.say: Customer money had been used by its sister trading firm.
When a report exposed the problem, users rushed to withdraw, and the money wasn't there.
Its founder was convicted of fraud and sentenced to twenty-five years in prison.
Lesson: big names and celebrity ads don't prove safety. Hold your own keys.
Follow for part 316: the efficient market idea. Not financial advice.
Can anyone beat the market consistently? One famous theory says almost nobody can.
scenes.p: The wolf tries to outrun a giant glowing scoreboard rolling after him on a racetrack, out of breath.

scenes.say: It's the efficient market idea: prices quickly reflect all available information.
If that's true, finding underpriced stocks consistently is extremely hard.
Markets aren't perfectly efficient. Bubbles and panics prove it.
But it explains why low-cost index funds are so hard to beat.
Follow for part 317: the day Bitcoin ETFs were approved. Not financial advice.

317.intro_say: How to invest in crypto. Part 317.

scenes.say: January 10th, 2024. The day Bitcoin entered Wall Street.
scenes.p: The wolf stands on the balcony of a classic stock exchange as a giant golden Bitcoin is raised like a flag, confetti everywhere.

Trading started the next day, and billions of dollars flowed in within weeks.
BlackRock's fund became one of the fastest-growing ETFs in history.
It made Bitcoin easier to buy for millions of people, and tied it closer to traditional finance.
